# Fourier analysis {#sec-fourier-analysis}

Fourier analysis decomposes a function into modes: a periodic function into the harmonics $e^{inx}$, a function
on the line into the plane waves $e^{ikx}$, a function on the sphere into the spherical harmonics $Y_{lm}$, and a
function on a compact group into the matrix coefficients of its irreducible representations. In each case the modes
are the eigenfunctions of a Laplacian, they are orthogonal for a natural inner product, the coefficients of a
function are inner products with the modes, and the sum of the squares of the coefficients is the square of the
norm of the function. The chapter develops this circle of ideas in four sections. Fourier series treats periodic
functions on the circle, their coefficients, the Dirichlet kernel and the Gibbs phenomenon, the convergence
theorems and Parseval's identity, with the square wave and the sawtooth as running examples. The Fourier transform
passes from the circle to the line, with the Gaussian as the central example, the convolution theorem, Plancherel's
theorem and the uncertainty inequality, which says that a function and its transform cannot both be narrow.
Distributions gives a meaning to the delta function and its derivatives, to the Fourier transform of $1$ and of
$\delta$, and to the principal value $1/x$, the objects that make the formal manipulations of the first two sections
rigorous. Harmonic analysis on the sphere and on compact groups describes the spherical harmonics as
eigenfunctions of the Laplacian on $S^2$ and as the spin-$l$ representations of $SU(2)$, states the Peter-Weyl
theorem, and ends with the mode expansion of a function on a coset space $G/H$, the general setting in which a
field on a compact space is expanded in modes. Each definition is followed by three examples of increasing
complexity and three exercises of increasing difficulty with hidden solutions; each section ends with a
proposition that collects its explicit values, and the quoted theorems (Dirichlet's
convergence theorem, Plancherel, the uncertainty inequality, Peter-Weyl) are stated with their hypotheses and
argued in the text. The real analysis assumed is that of @sec-series, @sec-riemann-integral and
@sec-multiple-integrals, the complex analysis that of @sec-contour-integration and @sec-residues, the orthogonal
functions and the delta of @sec-sturm-liouville and @sec-greens-functions, and the representation theory of $SU(2)$
that of @sec-weights-su2; the normalisations fixed here, $\hat f(k) = \int f(x)e^{-ikx}dx$ with inverse $f(x) =
\frac{1}{2\pi}\int\hat f(k)e^{ikx}dk$ and $c_n = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}f(x)e^{-inx}dx$ on the circle, are used
throughout the book.

## Fourier series {#sec-fourier-series}

A function on the circle is a periodic function on the line, and the harmonics $e^{inx}$ are the simplest periodic
functions of all. This section defines periodic functions and their Fourier coefficients, studies the partial sums
through the Dirichlet kernel, states the convergence theorems of Dirichlet and of the $L^2$ theory, and proves
Parseval's identity, with the square wave and the sawtooth of @fig-fourier-square-wave as running examples whose
coefficients, partial sums and overshoot are collected in @prp-fourier-series-values.

$x$ (right) on $(-\pi, \pi)$. The sums converge to the function away from the jumps, to the midpoint $0$ at the
jumps, and overshoot by about $9\%$ of the jump next to it however many terms are taken: the Gibbs phenomenon, with
the limiting overshoot $1.179$ marked. Generated by

### Periodic functions

Before anything can be expanded in harmonics one needs the class of functions that live on the circle. The
definition below fixes periodicity, the standard period $2\pi$, the way a function on an interval is extended, and
the finite sums of harmonics that will approximate everything else.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-periodic-function}
#### Periodic function

A function $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{C}$ is **periodic** with period $T > 0$ if $f(x + T) = f(x)$ for all $x$; it
is then determined by its values on any interval of length $T$, and after the rescaling $x \mapsto 2\pi x/T$ one
may take $T = 2\pi$, which is assumed from now on. A $2\pi$-periodic function is the same thing as a function on
the circle $S^1 = \mathbb{R}/2\pi\mathbb{Z}$, and a function given on $[0, 2\pi)$ or on $(-\pi, \pi]$ has a unique
**periodic extension**. A **trigonometric polynomial** of degree $N$ is a finite sum $\sum_{|n| \leq N} c_n
e^{inx}$, equivalently $\frac{a_0}{2} + \sum_{n=1}^N (a_n\cos nx + b_n\sin nx)$; a periodic function is **piecewise
continuous** if it has at most finitely many jumps per period, with one-sided limits $f(x^\pm)$ at each, and
**piecewise $C^1$** if the same holds for $f'$.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The harmonics themselves are the first periodic functions to look at, and the only subtlety is which period one
means. The first example records that $e^{inx}$ has the smaller period $2\pi/n$ as well as $2\pi$, which is why all
harmonics live on the same circle.

::: {#exm-fs-periodic-basic}
#### The harmonics

$\sin nx$, $\cos nx$ and $e^{inx}$ are $2\pi$-periodic for every integer $n$, and $2\pi/|n|$ is their smallest
period when $n \neq 0$: a function with period $T$ also has period $kT$ for every positive integer $k$. The
constant function is periodic with every period, and $e^{inx} = \cos nx + i\sin nx$ relates the complex and the
real harmonics.
:::

Extending a function from an interval produces jumps unless the values at the two ends agree, and these jumps
govern everything about convergence later on. The second example introduces the two running functions of the
section and locates their discontinuities.

::: {#exm-fs-periodic-extension}
#### The square wave and the sawtooth

The **square wave** is the periodic extension of $\operatorname{sgn} x$ from $(-\pi, \pi)$, and the **sawtooth**
that of $f(x) = x$ from $(-\pi, \pi)$ (@fig-fourier-square-wave). Both are piecewise $C^1$: the square wave jumps
by $2$ at every multiple of $\pi$, the sawtooth by $-2\pi$ at the odd multiples of $\pi$, where $f(\pi^-) = \pi$
and $f(\pi^+) = -\pi$. The extension of $|x|$ from $(-\pi, \pi)$ is continuous, since $|{-\pi}| = |\pi|$, but its
derivative jumps at the multiples of $\pi$.
:::

Some periodic functions are already trigonometric polynomials in disguise, and recognising them is a matter of
trigonometric identities. The third example rewrites a power of the cosine, which is the computation that
Euler's formula makes mechanical.

::: {#exm-fs-trig-polynomial}
#### $\cos^3 x$ as a trigonometric polynomial

With $\cos x = (e^{ix} + e^{-ix})/2$, the binomial theorem gives $\cos^3 x = \tfrac18(e^{3ix} + 3e^{ix} +
3e^{-ix} + e^{-3ix}) = \tfrac34\cos x + \tfrac14\cos 3x$, a trigonometric polynomial of degree $3$. Its Fourier
series is this finite sum and nothing else, as the orthogonality of the harmonics will show
(@def-fourier-coefficient).
:::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
Deciding whether a sum of periodic functions is periodic is a question about the ratio of the periods, and the
answer is negative when the ratio is irrational. The first exercise works this out, which is also the reason why
only integer multiples of a basic frequency appear in a Fourier series.

::: {#exr-fs-period-sum}
#### Periods of sums

Show that $\sin x + \sin 2x$ is $2\pi$-periodic, that $\sin x + \sin(x/2)$ has smallest period $4\pi$, and that
$\sin x + \sin\sqrt2\,x$ is not periodic at all.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Both terms of the first sum have period $2\pi$. For the second, $\sin(x/2)$ has smallest period $4\pi$ and $\sin
x$ has period $4\pi$ too, so the sum has period $4\pi$; it has no smaller one, since a period $T$ of the sum
would give $\sin(x + T) + \sin((x + T)/2) = \sin x + \sin(x/2)$ for all $x$, and comparing the values at $x = 0$
and the second derivatives at $x = 0$ forces $\sin T + \sin(T/2) = 0$ and $\sin T + \tfrac14\sin(T/2) = 0$,
hence $\sin T = \sin(T/2) = 0$ and $T \in 4\pi\mathbb{Z}$. For the third, a period $T$ would make $f(x) = \sin x +
\sin\sqrt2 x$ satisfy $f(T) = f(0) = 0$ and $f''(T) = 0$, that is, $\sin T + \sin\sqrt2 T = 0$ and $\sin T +
2\sin\sqrt2 T = 0$, so $\sin T = \sin\sqrt2 T = 0$, $T = m\pi$ and $\sqrt2 T = n\pi$ with integers $m, n \neq 0$,
contradicting the irrationality of $\sqrt2$.
:::

::: {#exr-fs-cos-power}
#### $\cos^4 x$ as a trigonometric polynomial

Express $\cos^4 x$ and $\sin^3 x$ as trigonometric polynomials and check the identities with Sage.

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\cos^4 x = \tfrac1{16}(e^{ix} + e^{-ix})^4 = \tfrac1{16}(e^{4ix} + 4e^{2ix} + 6 + 4e^{-2ix} + e^{-4ix}) = \tfrac38 +
\tfrac12\cos 2x + \tfrac18\cos 4x$, and $\sin^3 x = \tfrac34\sin x - \tfrac14\sin 3x$. Sage's `trig_reduce`
produces the same expansions:

A periodic function integrated over any interval of one period gives the same number, which is what makes the
coefficients below independent of the interval chosen. The third exercise proves this and uses it to show that
the integral of a product of two periodic functions is a periodic function of the shift between them.

::: {#exr-fs-periodic-integral}
#### Integrals over a period

Prove that $\int_a^{a + 2\pi} f(x)\,dx$ is independent of $a$ for a piecewise continuous $2\pi$-periodic $f$, and
deduce that $F(t) = \int_0^{2\pi} f(x)g(x - t)\,dx$ is $2\pi$-periodic in $t$ for periodic $f, g$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\frac{d}{da}\int_a^{a + 2\pi} f = f(a + 2\pi) - f(a) = 0$ at every point where $f$ is continuous, by the
fundamental theorem of calculus (@sec-riemann-integral), and the integral is a continuous function of $a$, so it
is constant. For $F$, substitute $y = x - t$: $F(t) = \int_{-t}^{2\pi - t} f(y + t)g(y)\,dy$, and $y \mapsto f(y +
t)g(y)$ is periodic, so by the first part the integral equals $\int_0^{2\pi} f(y + t)g(y)\,dy$, which is visibly
$2\pi$-periodic in $t$. This is the periodicity of the convolution on the circle, the form in which the partial
sums are written in @def-fourier-partial-sum.
:::

### Fourier coefficients

The coefficients of a periodic function are its inner products with the harmonics, and everything rests on the
fact that distinct harmonics are orthogonal. The definition fixes the normalisation of the coefficients once and
for all, in the complex form and in the real form, and records the orthogonality relation that makes them the
right numbers.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-fourier-coefficient}
#### Fourier coefficient

The **Fourier coefficients** of a piecewise continuous $2\pi$-periodic $f$ are
$$
c_n = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi} f(x)\,e^{-inx}\,dx, \qquad n \in \mathbb{Z},
$$
and the **Fourier series** of $f$ is $\sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} c_n e^{inx}$, written $f \sim \sum c_n e^{inx}$ until
its convergence is settled. In real form $f \sim \frac{a_0}{2} + \sum_{n \geq 1}(a_n\cos nx + b_n\sin nx)$ with
$a_n = \frac1\pi\int_0^{2\pi} f(x)\cos nx\,dx$ and $b_n = \frac1\pi\int_0^{2\pi} f(x)\sin nx\,dx$, related by $c_n =
\tfrac12(a_n - ib_n)$ and $c_{-n} = \tfrac12(a_n + ib_n)$ for $n \geq 1$, $c_0 = a_0/2$. The coefficients are the
inner products $c_n = \langle e^{inx}, f\rangle/2\pi$ for $\langle g, f\rangle = \int_0^{2\pi}\bar g f\,dx$, and the
**orthogonality of the modes**
$$
\int_0^{2\pi} e^{inx}\,e^{-imx}\,dx = 2\pi\,\delta_{nm}
$$ {#eq-mode-orthogonality}
shows that the coefficients of a trigonometric polynomial are its given coefficients and that $c_n$ is the unique
choice making $f - c_n e^{inx}$ orthogonal to $e^{inx}$ (@def-orthogonal-functions).
:::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The square wave is odd, so only sines appear, and the integral giving $b_n$ is elementary. The first example
computes it and finds the slow $1/n$ decay that goes with a jump.

::: {#exm-fs-coefficients-square}
#### The square wave

For the square wave, $a_n = 0$ by oddness and $b_n = \frac2\pi\int_0^\pi\sin nx\,dx = \frac{2}{\pi n}(1 - \cos
n\pi)$, which is $4/(\pi n)$ for odd $n$ and $0$ for even $n$ (@prp-fourier-series-values). So
$$
\operatorname{sgn} x \sim \frac4\pi\Bigl(\sin x + \frac{\sin 3x}{3} + \frac{\sin 5x}{5} + \dots\Bigr),
$$
with coefficients decaying like $1/n$: the series does not converge absolutely.
:::

The sawtooth is also odd, and an integration by parts gives its coefficients with an alternating sign. The
second example shows the same $1/n$ decay, again the signature of a jump in the periodic extension.

::: {#exm-fs-coefficients-sawtooth}
#### The sawtooth

For $f(x) = x$ on $(-\pi, \pi)$, $b_n = \frac1\pi\int_{-\pi}^\pi x\sin nx\,dx = \frac1\pi\Bigl[-\frac{x\cos
nx}{n}\Bigr]_{-\pi}^{\pi} + \frac{1}{\pi n}\int_{-\pi}^\pi\cos nx\,dx = \frac{2(-1)^{n+1}}{n}$, so $x \sim
2\bigl(\sin x - \tfrac12\sin 2x + \tfrac13\sin 3x - \dots\bigr)$ (@prp-fourier-series-values). Since the function
jumps by $-2\pi$ at $\pm\pi$, the coefficients again decay like $1/n$.
:::

A continuous function with a kink has coefficients decaying one power faster, and a smooth function has rapidly
decaying coefficients. The third example contrasts $|x|$ with a trigonometric polynomial to make the rule
"smoothness equals decay" visible, which @exr-fs-coefficients-decay proves.

::: {#exm-fs-coefficients-smooth}
#### Decay and smoothness

For $f(x) = |x|$ on $(-\pi, \pi)$, which is continuous with a kink, $b_n = 0$ by evenness, $a_0 = \pi$ and $a_n =
\frac2\pi\int_0^\pi x\cos nx\,dx = \frac{2}{\pi n^2}(\cos n\pi - 1)$, equal to $-4/(\pi n^2)$ for odd $n$ and $0$
for even $n$ (@exr-fs-coefficients-abs): the decay is $1/n^2$. For the smooth function $\cos^3 x$ all coefficients
beyond $n = 3$ vanish (@exm-fs-trig-polynomial), and for $e^{\cos x}$ one finds $c_n = I_n(1)$, a modified Bessel
function, decaying faster than any power of $n$.
:::

::: {#exr-fs-coefficients-abs}
#### The coefficients of $|x|$

Compute the Fourier coefficients of the periodic extension of $|x|$ from $(-\pi, \pi)$, write the series, and

\frac2\pi\Bigl(\Bigl[\frac{x\sin nx}{n}\Bigr]_0^\pi - \int_0^\pi\frac{\sin nx}{n}dx\Bigr) = \frac{2(\cos n\pi -
1)}{\pi n^2}$, so
$$
|x| \sim \frac\pi2 - \frac4\pi\Bigl(\cos x + \frac{\cos 3x}{9} + \frac{\cos 5x}{25} + \dots\Bigr).
$$

The complex and the real forms of the series carry the same information, and the dictionary between them is used
silently whenever one switches. The second exercise derives the dictionary and the symmetry $c_{-n} = \bar c_n$
of real functions.

::: {#exr-fs-coefficients-complex-real}
#### Complex and real coefficients

Derive $c_n = \tfrac12(a_n - ib_n)$ and $c_{-n} = \tfrac12(a_n + ib_n)$ for $n \geq 1$, show that $f$ is real if
and only if $c_{-n} = \bar c_n$ for all $n$, and that $f$ is even (odd) if and only if all $b_n$ (all $a_n$)
vanish.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$e^{-inx} = \cos nx - i\sin nx$ gives $2\pi c_n = \pi a_n - i\pi b_n$ directly, and $n \to -n$ changes the sign of
the sine term. If $f$ is real, $\overline{c_n} = \frac1{2\pi}\int f e^{inx} = c_{-n}$; conversely $c_{-n} = \bar
c_n$ makes $a_n = c_n + c_{-n}$ and $b_n = i(c_n - c_{-n})$ real, and then the partial sums are real, so $f$ is
real wherever the series converges to it (@thm-fourier-convergence). For even $f$ the integrand $f(x)\sin nx$ is
odd over $(-\pi, \pi)$, so $b_n = 0$; for odd $f$, $f(x)\cos nx$ is odd and $a_n = 0$; conversely a series with
only cosines (sines) is even (odd).
:::

The rule that smoother functions have faster-decaying coefficients is a repeated integration by parts, and the
same computation gives the coefficients of the derivative. The third exercise asks for both, including the
boundary terms that appear when the function is not continuous.

::: {#exr-fs-coefficients-decay}
#### Decay of the coefficients

Show that if $f$ is continuous, $2\pi$-periodic and piecewise $C^1$ then the coefficients of $f'$ are $in\,c_n$
and $|c_n| \leq C/|n|$; that if $f$ is $C^k$ then $|c_n| \leq C_k/|n|^k$; and compute the boundary term that
appears for the sawtooth, where $f$ jumps.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Integrating by parts over $[0, 2\pi]$, $\int f'e^{-inx}dx = [fe^{-inx}]_0^{2\pi} + in\int fe^{-inx}dx = 2\pi
in\,c_n$, the boundary term vanishing by continuity and periodicity; so $c_n(f') = in\,c_n(f)$, and $|c_n| =
|c_n(f')|/|n| \leq \frac{1}{2\pi|n|}\int|f'|$. For a $C^k$ function iterate $k$ times. For the sawtooth on $(-\pi,
\pi)$, $f' = 1$ has all coefficients zero for $n \neq 0$, but the boundary term is $[xe^{-inx}]_{-\pi}^{\pi} =
2\pi(-1)^n$, so $0 = 2\pi(-1)^n + 2\pi in\,c_n$ and $c_n = i(-1)^n/n$, that is, $b_n = i(c_n - c_{-n}) =
2(-1)^{n+1}/n$ as in @exm-fs-coefficients-sawtooth: the jump is what produces the $1/n$ decay.
:::

### Partial sums

Whether and how the series represents the function is decided by its partial sums, and the partial sums have a
closed form as an integral of the function against a kernel. The definition introduces the Dirichlet kernel,
records its two properties, and names the overshoot visible in @fig-fourier-square-wave.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-fourier-partial-sum}
#### Partial Fourier sum

The **partial Fourier sum** of order $N$ of $f$ is $S_N f(x) = \sum_{|n| \leq N} c_n e^{inx}$. Inserting the
coefficients and exchanging sum and integral,
$$
S_N f(x) = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi} D_N(x - y)\,f(y)\,dy, \qquad D_N(t) = \sum_{|n| \leq N} e^{int} =
\frac{\sin\bigl((N + \tfrac12)t\bigr)}{\sin(t/2)},
$$ {#eq-dirichlet-kernel}
where $D_N$ is the **Dirichlet kernel**: an even trigonometric polynomial with $\frac1{2\pi}\int_{-\pi}^\pi D_N =
1$ and $D_N(0) = 2N + 1$, which concentrates at $0$ as $N$ grows but is not positive and has $\int_{-\pi}^\pi|D_N|
\to \infty$ like $\log N$. Near a jump of $f$ the partial sums overshoot the one-sided limit by a fixed fraction of
the jump that does not decrease with $N$, the **Gibbs phenomenon**.
:::

#### Partial sums of the square wave

the jump, and their first maximum, at $x = \pi/(N + 1)$, stays near $1.179$ as $N$ grows: an overshoot of about
$9\%$ of the jump of size $2$.

The Dirichlet kernel for a small $N$ can be written out and its properties verified by hand. The second example
does this for $N = 3$ and explains why the kernel's sign changes are the source of all the difficulties of
pointwise convergence.

::: {#exm-fs-dirichlet-kernel}
#### The Dirichlet kernel $D_3$

$D_3(t) = 1 + 2\cos t + 2\cos 2t + 2\cos 3t = \sin(7t/2)/\sin(t/2)$, with $D_3(0) = 7$ and
$\int_{-\pi}^\pi D_3 = 2\pi$ (@prp-fourier-series-values). It oscillates with zeros at $t = 2\pi k/7$, taking
negative values between them; because of these negative lobes $S_N f$ is not an average of $f$, and a function
can have $S_N f(x) \to \infty$ at a point even though it is continuous (@exm-fs-convergence-du-bois).
:::

The overshoot has an exact limiting value, obtained by evaluating the partial sum at its first maximum and
recognising a Riemann sum. The third example carries out this classical computation, whose value is one of the
items of @prp-fourier-series-values.

::: {#exm-fs-gibbs-constant}
#### The Gibbs constant

For the square wave, $S_N'(x) = \frac4\pi\sum_{\text{odd } n \leq N}\cos nx = \frac{2\sin((N + 1)x)}{\pi\sin x}$
for odd $N$, so the first maximum after $0$ is at $x_N = \pi/(N + 1)$, and
$$
S_N(x_N) = \frac4\pi\sum_{\text{odd } n \leq N}\frac{\sin(n\pi/(N + 1))}{n} \;\longrightarrow\;
\frac2\pi\int_0^\pi\frac{\sin t}{t}\,dt = \frac2\pi\operatorname{Si}(\pi) = 1.17898\ldots,
$$
a Riemann sum (@def-riemann-integral) with step $2\pi/(N + 1)$. The overshoot is $0.179$, about $9\%$ of the
jump $2$, and $S_{199}(\pi/200) = 1.1790$ to three decimals (@prp-fourier-series-values).
:::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The closed form of the Dirichlet kernel is a geometric sum, and its two properties follow from the sum and from
the orthogonality relation. The first exercise asks for the derivation, which is the only computation needed to
analyse pointwise convergence.

::: {#exr-fs-dirichlet-closed-form}
#### The closed form of $D_N$

Derive $\sum_{|n| \leq N} e^{int} = \sin((N + \tfrac12)t)/\sin(t/2)$, and show that $\frac1{2\pi}\int_{-\pi}^\pi
D_N = 1$ and $D_N(0) = 2N + 1$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
With $q = e^{it} \neq 1$, $\sum_{n=-N}^N q^n = q^{-N}\frac{q^{2N+1} - 1}{q - 1} = \frac{q^{N + 1/2} - q^{-N -
1/2}}{q^{1/2} - q^{-1/2}} = \frac{2i\sin((N + \tfrac12)t)}{2i\sin(t/2)}$. Integrating the sum term by term, only
$n = 0$ survives by @eq-mode-orthogonality, giving $2\pi$; at $t = 0$ every term is $1$ and there are $2N + 1$ of
them, in agreement with the limit $\sin((N + \tfrac12)t)/\sin(t/2) \to (2N + 1)$ as $t \to 0$.
:::

Replacing the partial sums by their averages removes the negative lobes of the kernel and with them the Gibbs
phenomenon. The third exercise introduces the Fejér kernel and proves its positivity, the key to Fejér's theorem
that the averaged sums of every continuous function converge uniformly.

::: {#exr-fs-fejer}
#### The Fejér kernel

Define the Cesàro means $\sigma_N f = \frac{1}{N + 1}\sum_{n=0}^N S_n f$. Show that $\sigma_N f = \frac1{2\pi}\int
F_N(x - y)f(y)\,dy$ with $F_N(t) = \frac{1}{N + 1}\sum_{n=0}^N D_n(t) = \frac{1}{N + 1}\frac{\sin^2((N +
1)t/2)}{\sin^2(t/2)}$, that $F_N \geq 0$ with $\frac1{2\pi}\int F_N = 1$, and deduce that $|\sigma_N f| \leq
\sup|f|$: the Cesàro means never overshoot.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Averaging the integral formula for $S_n f$ gives the one for $\sigma_N f$ with the averaged kernel. With $s =
\sin(t/2)$, $\sum_{n=0}^N\sin((n + \tfrac12)t) = \operatorname{Im}\sum_n e^{i(n + 1/2)t} =
\operatorname{Im}\frac{e^{it/2}(e^{i(N+1)t} - 1)}{e^{it} - 1} = \operatorname{Im}\frac{e^{i(N+1)t} -
1}{2is} = \frac{1 - \cos((N + 1)t)}{2s} = \frac{\sin^2((N + 1)t/2)}{s}$, and dividing by $(N + 1)s$ gives $F_N$,
visibly non-negative. Its integral is the average of the integrals of the $D_n$, each $2\pi$. Then $|\sigma_N
f(x)| \leq \frac1{2\pi}\int F_N(x - y)|f(y)|\,dy \leq \sup|f|$, since $F_N \geq 0$ integrates to $2\pi$. A
positive kernel of unit mass concentrating at $0$ is an approximate identity, and $\sigma_N f \to f$ uniformly
for continuous $f$ (Fejér's theorem), with no Gibbs overshoot.
:::

### Convergence

The question of when the Fourier series equals the function has several answers depending on what one asks of
$f$ and in what sense the limit is taken. The theorem below collects the three that are used throughout the book,
the pointwise theorem of Dirichlet, uniform convergence under absolute summability, and the $L^2$ theorem, with
the proof of the first sketched through the Dirichlet kernel.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#thm-fourier-convergence}
#### Convergence of Fourier series

Let $f$ be $2\pi$-periodic. (i) (Dirichlet) If $f$ is piecewise $C^1$, then $S_N f(x) \to \tfrac12\bigl(f(x^+) +
f(x^-)\bigr)$ at every $x$, in particular $S_N f(x) \to f(x)$ at points of continuity. (ii) If $\sum|c_n| <
\infty$, which holds when $f$ is continuous and piecewise $C^1$, the series converges absolutely and uniformly
(@def-uniform-convergence) to a continuous function, which equals $f$ at its points of continuity. (iii) (Riesz-Fischer) If
$\int_0^{2\pi}|f|^2 < \infty$ then $\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}|f - S_N f|^2\,dx \to 0$, and conversely every
square-summable sequence $(c_n)$ is the coefficient sequence of such an $f$; Carleson's theorem adds that the series
of a square-integrable function converges to it at almost every point. *Sketch of (i).* By @eq-dirichlet-kernel and
the evenness of $D_N$, $S_N f(x) - \tfrac12(f(x^+) + f(x^-)) = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^\pi D_N(t)\bigl[f(x + t) +
f(x - t) - f(x^+) - f(x^-)\bigr]dt$; the bracket divided by $\sin(t/2)$ is piecewise continuous on $[0, \pi]$
because $f$ is piecewise $C^1$, so the integral is a Fourier coefficient of a piecewise continuous function at
frequency $N + \tfrac12$ and tends to $0$ by the Riemann-Lebesgue lemma (@exr-fs-riemann-lebesgue). Statement
(ii) is the Weierstrass $M$-test (@sec-series), and (iii) follows from Parseval's identity (@thm-parseval).
:::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The square wave satisfies the hypotheses of Dirichlet's theorem, and its series shows both conclusions at once:
convergence to the function away from the jumps and to the midpoint at them. The first example records this, and
notes that the convergence cannot be uniform.

::: {#exm-fs-convergence-square}
#### The square wave at its jumps

The square wave is piecewise $C^1$, so its series converges to $\operatorname{sgn} x$ for $x \neq 0, \pm\pi$ and
to $\tfrac12(1 + (-1)) = 0$ at the jumps, which is what every partial sum gives there anyway since $\sin(n\cdot0) =
0$. The convergence is not uniform: a uniform limit of continuous functions is continuous (@def-uniform-convergence),
and the Gibbs overshoot of @exm-fs-gibbs-constant persists at a distance $\pi/(N + 1)$ from the jump.
:::

For a continuous piecewise $C^1$ function the series converges absolutely and uniformly, and evaluating it at a
convenient point yields the sum of a numerical series. The second example does this for $|x|$ and obtains
$\sum 1/(2k + 1)^2$.

::: {#exm-fs-convergence-abs}
#### $|x|$ and a sum of reciprocal odd squares

The series $\frac\pi2 - \frac4\pi\sum_{k \geq 0}\frac{\cos(2k + 1)x}{(2k + 1)^2}$ of $|x|$ (@exr-fs-coefficients-abs)
has $\sum|a_n| < \infty$, so it converges uniformly to $|x|$ on $[-\pi, \pi]$. At $x = 0$, $0 = \frac\pi2 -
\frac4\pi\sum_{k \geq 0}\frac{1}{(2k + 1)^2}$, that is, $1 + \frac19 + \frac1{25} + \dots = \frac{\pi^2}{8}$; at
$x = \pi$ the same identity returns, and at $x = \pi/2$ one finds $\sum_{k \geq 0}(-1)^k/(2k + 1)^2 = G$,
Catalan's constant.
:::

Continuity alone is not enough for pointwise convergence, and the reason is the Dirichlet kernel's growing
$L^1$ norm. The third example states du Bois-Reymond's counterexample without proof and contrasts it with
Fejér's theorem, so that the hypotheses of the theorem are seen to be necessary.

::: {#exm-fs-convergence-du-bois}
#### A continuous function with a divergent series

There exist continuous $2\pi$-periodic functions whose Fourier series diverges at a point (du Bois-Reymond, 1873);
the mechanism is that $\int_{-\pi}^\pi|D_N| \approx \frac{8}{\pi}\log N$ is unbounded, so the functionals $f
\mapsto S_N f(0)$ have unbounded norms on the continuous functions. For the same $f$ the Cesàro means converge
uniformly (@exr-fs-fejer), and Carleson's theorem guarantees convergence at almost every point. The piecewise
$C^1$ hypothesis of (i) excludes such functions and is what the physical examples of this book satisfy.
:::

Evaluating the square-wave series at a point where it is known to converge gives Leibniz's series for $\pi$. The
first exercise does this, and then uses Sage to see how slowly the partial sums approach $\pi/4$.

::: {#exr-fs-leibniz}
#### Leibniz's series from the square wave

Evaluate the Fourier series of the square wave at $x = \pi/2$ to obtain $\frac\pi4 = 1 - \frac13 + \frac15 -
\dots$, and compute partial sums in Sage to see the rate of convergence.

At $x = \pi/2$ the function is continuous with value $1$, and $\sin(n\pi/2) = (-1)^{(n-1)/2}$ for odd $n$, so
Dirichlet's theorem gives $1 = \frac4\pi(1 - \frac13 + \frac15 - \dots)$. The alternating series converges slowly,
the error after $N$ terms being about $1/(2N)$:

{{< sage exr-fs-leibniz >}}

The Riemann-Lebesgue lemma is the analytic engine of Dirichlet's theorem: the Fourier coefficients of an
integrable function tend to zero. The second exercise proves it for piecewise continuous functions by
approximation with step functions, the case needed above, where the frequency need not be an integer.

::: {#exr-fs-riemann-lebesgue}
#### The Riemann-Lebesgue lemma

Prove that $\int_a^b g(t)\sin(\lambda t)\,dt \to 0$ as $\lambda \to \infty$ for every piecewise continuous $g$ on
$[a, b]$, first for a step function and then in general.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
For $g = 1$ on $[c, d]$ the integral is $(\cos\lambda c - \cos\lambda d)/\lambda$, of absolute value at most
$2/\lambda$, so the statement holds for step functions. A piecewise continuous $g$ is Riemann integrable, so for
every $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a step function $s$ with $\int_a^b|g - s| < \varepsilon$ (@def-riemann-integral,
lower sums). Then $|\int g\sin\lambda t| \leq |\int (g - s)\sin\lambda t| + |\int s\sin\lambda t| \leq \varepsilon +
|\int s\sin\lambda t|$, and the second term is below $\varepsilon$ for $\lambda$ large; so the limit superior is
at most $2\varepsilon$ for every $\varepsilon$. The same argument works with $\cos\lambda t$ and $e^{i\lambda t}$,
and shows $c_n \to 0$ for every piecewise continuous periodic $f$.
:::

Differentiating a Fourier series term by term is legitimate when the result converges uniformly, and illegitimate
when it does not, even though both series look equally formal. The third exercise contrasts $|x|$, whose
differentiated series is the square wave, with the sawtooth, whose differentiated series diverges everywhere.

::: {#exr-fs-termwise-differentiation}
#### Term-by-term differentiation

Differentiate the series of $|x|$ term by term and identify the result; differentiate the series of the sawtooth
term by term and show that the resulting series diverges at every $x$; explain the difference through
@exr-fs-coefficients-decay.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Differentiating $\frac\pi2 - \frac4\pi\sum_k\frac{\cos(2k + 1)x}{(2k + 1)^2}$ gives $\frac4\pi\sum_k\frac{\sin(2k +
1)x}{2k + 1}$, the series of the square wave, which is indeed $\frac{d}{dx}|x| = \operatorname{sgn} x$: here $f$ is
continuous and piecewise $C^1$, so $c_n(f') = in\,c_n(f)$ and the differentiated series is the Fourier series of
$f'$, convergent by Dirichlet's theorem. Differentiating $2\sum(-1)^{n+1}\sin(nx)/n$ gives $2\sum(-1)^{n+1}\cos
nx$, whose terms do not tend to zero at any $x$, so the series diverges everywhere; the sawtooth is not continuous,
the boundary term of @exr-fs-coefficients-decay does not vanish, and the series of $f' = 1$ is not the
differentiated series. In the language of @sec-distributions, the derivative of the sawtooth is $1 -
2\pi\sum_k\delta(x - (2k + 1)\pi)$, and the divergent cosine series is the Fourier series of this comb of deltas.
:::

### Parseval's identity

The sum of the squares of the coefficients equals the mean square of the function, which is the Pythagorean
theorem in infinitely many dimensions. The theorem states this identity in both forms together with the finite
inequality of Bessel and the best-approximation property that explains why Fourier coefficients are the right
choice.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#thm-parseval}
#### Parseval's identity

For a $2\pi$-periodic $f$ with $\int_0^{2\pi}|f|^2 < \infty$,
$$
\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}|f(x)|^2\,dx = \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}}|c_n|^2, \qquad \frac1\pi\int_0^{2\pi}|f|^2\,dx =
\frac{|a_0|^2}{2} + \sum_{n \geq 1}\bigl(|a_n|^2 + |b_n|^2\bigr),
$$ {#eq-parseval}
and more generally $\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\bar f g\,dx = \sum_n\bar c_n(f)c_n(g)$. *Argument.* For a
trigonometric polynomial $T = \sum_{|n| \leq N} t_n e^{inx}$, @eq-mode-orthogonality gives $\frac{1}{2\pi}\int|f -
T|^2 = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int|f|^2 - \sum_{|n| \leq N}|c_n|^2 + \sum_{|n| \leq N}|c_n - t_n|^2$, so $S_N f$ is the *
*best approximation** of $f$ in mean square among trigonometric polynomials of degree $N$, and **Bessel's
inequality** $\sum_{|n| \leq N}|c_n|^2 \leq \frac{1}{2\pi}\int|f|^2$ holds for every $N$. Equality in the limit is
the statement that $\frac{1}{2\pi}\int|f - S_N f|^2 \to 0$, which holds because trigonometric polynomials
approximate every such $f$ in mean square (by Fejér's theorem for continuous $f$ and by approximation of $f$ with
continuous functions in general); the polarised form follows by applying the identity to $f + g$ and $f + ig$.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
Parseval's identity turns the computation of a Fourier series into the evaluation of a numerical series, and the
sawtooth gives the most famous one. The first example obtains Euler's sum $\sum 1/n^2 = \pi^2/6$, one of the
items of @prp-fourier-series-values.

::: {#exm-fs-parseval-basel}
#### $\sum 1/n^2 = \pi^2/6$

For the sawtooth, $\frac1\pi\int_{-\pi}^\pi x^2\,dx = \frac{2\pi^2}{3}$ and $b_n = 2(-1)^{n+1}/n$, so
@eq-parseval reads $\frac{2\pi^2}{3} = \sum_{n \geq 1}\frac{4}{n^2}$, that is, $\sum_{n \geq 1}\frac{1}{n^2} =
\frac{\pi^2}{6}$ (@prp-fourier-series-values), Euler's solution of the Basel problem obtained in @sec-series by a
different route.
:::

Applying the identity to a function with faster-decaying coefficients gives sums of higher reciprocal powers.
The second example uses $|x|$ and obtains a sum of reciprocal fourth powers, to be compared with the sum from
the convergence theorem.

::: {#exm-fs-parseval-abs}
#### $\sum 1/(2k + 1)^4 = \pi^4/96$

For $|x|$ on $(-\pi, \pi)$, $\frac1\pi\int_{-\pi}^\pi x^2 = \frac{2\pi^2}{3}$, $a_0 = \pi$ and $a_{2k+1} = -
4/(\pi(2k + 1)^2)$, so $\frac{2\pi^2}{3} = \frac{\pi^2}{2} + \frac{16}{\pi^2}\sum_{k \geq 0}\frac{1}{(2k + 1)^4}$,
giving $\sum_{k \geq 0}(2k + 1)^{-4} = \frac{\pi^4}{96}$; with the even terms, $\zeta(4) = \frac{\pi^4}{96}\cdot
\frac{16}{15} = \frac{\pi^4}{90}$ (@exr-fs-zeta4).
:::

For a trigonometric polynomial the identity is a finite computation, and the best-approximation property can be
seen directly. The third example takes $\cos^3 x$ and shows that dropping its $\cos 3x$ term is the best one can
do with degree $1$.

::: {#exm-fs-bessel-inequality}
#### Bessel's inequality for a trigonometric polynomial

For $f = \cos^3 x = \tfrac34\cos x + \tfrac14\cos 3x$, Parseval gives $\frac1\pi\int_0^{2\pi}\cos^6 x\,dx =
\tfrac9{16} + \tfrac1{16} = \tfrac58$, which the integral confirms. The best mean-square approximation by a
trigonometric polynomial of degree $1$ is $S_1 f = \tfrac34\cos x$, with error $\frac{1}{2\pi}\int|f - S_1 f|^2 =
\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac1{16} = \tfrac1{32}$; any other choice $t\cos x$ has error $\tfrac1{32} + \tfrac12(t -
\tfrac34)^2$, and Bessel's inequality $\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac9{16} \leq \tfrac58$ is strict because the degree-$3$
term is missing.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The square wave gives a third numerical series by Parseval, and comparing it with the sum from $|x|$ is a
consistency check. The first exercise asks for the computation and for the same sums evaluated in Sage.

::: {#exr-fs-parseval-square}
#### Parseval for the square wave

Apply Parseval's identity to the square wave, deduce $\sum_{k \geq 0}\frac{1}{(2k + 1)^2} = \frac{\pi^2}{8}$ and
hence $\sum_{n \geq 1}\frac{1}{n^2} = \frac{\pi^2}{6}$ again, and check with Sage.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\frac1\pi\int_{-\pi}^\pi(\operatorname{sgn} x)^2\,dx = 2 = \sum_{\text{odd } n}\frac{16}{\pi^2 n^2}$, so
$\sum_{\text{odd } n} n^{-2} = \pi^2/8$, as in @exm-fs-convergence-abs. The even $n$ contribute
$\tfrac14\sum_n n^{-2}$, so $\sum_n n^{-2} = \frac{\pi^2}{8}\cdot\frac43 = \frac{\pi^2}{6}$:

{{< sage exr-fs-parseval-square >}}
:::

The best-approximation identity is the heart of the argument for Parseval and deserves its own derivation. The
second exercise expands the mean-square error of an arbitrary trigonometric polynomial and reads off the two
consequences.

::: {#exr-fs-best-approximation}
#### Best approximation in mean square

Prove that $\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}|f - \sum_{|n| \leq N}t_n e^{inx}|^2\,dx = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int|f|^2 -
\sum_{|n| \leq N}|c_n|^2 + \sum_{|n| \leq N}|c_n - t_n|^2$, and deduce Bessel's inequality and that the error is
minimised exactly when $t_n = c_n$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Expanding $|f - T|^2 = |f|^2 - \bar fT - f\bar T + |T|^2$ and integrating, $\frac{1}{2\pi}\int\bar fT = \sum t_n\bar
c_n$ by the definition of $c_n$, and $\frac{1}{2\pi}\int|T|^2 = \sum|t_n|^2$ by @eq-mode-orthogonality; so the
error is $\frac{1}{2\pi}\int|f|^2 - \sum(t_n\bar c_n + \bar t_nc_n - |t_n|^2) = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int|f|^2 -
\sum|c_n|^2 + \sum|c_n - t_n|^2$ after completing the square. The last sum is non-negative and zero only for $t_n
= c_n$, which gives the minimality; taking $t_n = c_n$ and using that the error is non-negative gives Bessel's
inequality.
:::

The sums of reciprocal even powers of the integers all come out of Parseval applied to powers of $x$, and the
pattern continues with Bernoulli numbers. The third exercise obtains $\zeta(2)$ and $\zeta(4)$ from $x^2$, with
the integrals and sums done by Sage.

::: {#exr-fs-zeta4}
#### $\zeta(2)$ and $\zeta(4)$ from $x^2$

Compute the Fourier coefficients of $x^2$ on $(-\pi, \pi)$, evaluate the series at $x = \pi$ to get $\zeta(2)$,
and apply Parseval to get $\zeta(4) = \pi^4/90$; check everything in Sage.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$a_0 = \frac{2\pi^2}{3}$, $a_n = \frac{4(-1)^n}{n^2}$, $b_n = 0$, so $x^2 = \frac{\pi^2}{3} + 4\sum_n\frac{(-1)^n\cos
nx}{n^2}$, uniformly convergent. At $x = \pi$: $\pi^2 = \frac{\pi^2}{3} + 4\zeta(2)$, so $\zeta(2) = \pi^2/6$.
Parseval: $\frac1\pi\int_{-\pi}^\pi x^4 = \frac{2\pi^4}{5} = \frac{2\pi^4}{9} + 16\zeta(4)$, so $\zeta(4) =
\frac{\pi^4}{16}\bigl(\frac25 - \frac29\bigr) = \frac{\pi^4}{90}$:

{{< sage exr-fs-zeta4 >}}
:::

### Worked computations

The computations of this section, the orthogonality integral, the coefficients of the two running waves,
Parseval's evaluation of $\sum 1/n^2$, the Dirichlet kernel, an $L^2$ error and the Gibbs constant, are collected
in one proposition. Every item is an exact integral or a finite sum, and the three examples that follow work out
the coefficients, the $L^2$ error and the Gibbs constant in detail.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-fourier-series-values}
#### Fourier series of the square wave and the sawtooth

$\int_0^{2\pi}e^{inx}e^{-imx}dx = 2\pi\delta_{nm}$ for $|n|, |m| \leq 3$; the square wave has $a_n = 0$ and $b_n =
4/(\pi n)$ for odd $n$, $0$ for even $n$, and the sawtooth $a_n = 0$, $b_n = 2(-1)^{n+1}/n$ ($n \leq 6$); Parseval
for the sawtooth gives $\sum 1/n^2 = \pi^2/6$; $S_5$ of the square wave is $\frac4\pi(\sin x + \tfrac13\sin 3x +
\tfrac15\sin 5x)$; $D_3(x) = \sin(7x/2)/\sin(x/2)$ with $\int_{-\pi}^\pi D_3 = 2\pi$; $\int_{-\pi}^\pi(f -
S_9f)^2 = 2\pi - \pi\sum_{\text{odd } n \leq 9}(4/\pi n)^2 = 0.2538\ldots$ for the square wave; and $S_{199}(\pi/200)
= 1.1790$ agrees with $\frac2\pi\operatorname{Si}(\pi) = 1.17897974\ldots$ to $10^{-3}$.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The coefficients of a function with jumps are sums of integrals over the pieces on which it is smooth. The first
example computes them for the square wave and explains why they are exact rational multiples of $1/\pi$.

::: {#exm-fs-sage-piecewise}
#### Coefficients of piecewise functions

The square wave is $-1$ on $(-\pi, 0)$ and $1$ on $(0, \pi)$, so $a_n = 0$ by oddness and $b_n =
\frac1\pi\bigl(-\int_{-\pi}^0\sin nx\,dx + \int_0^\pi\sin nx\,dx\bigr)$. Each of the two integrals equals
$(1 - \cos n\pi)/n$, an integer divided by $n$, so $b_n = \frac{2(1 - (-1)^n)}{\pi n}$ is a rational multiple of
$1/\pi$: $4/(\pi n)$ for odd $n$, for instance $4/(3\pi)$ for $n = 3$, and $0$ for even $n$. Summing up to $N = 5$
gives $S_5 = \frac4\pi(\sin x + \tfrac13\sin 3x + \tfrac15\sin 5x)$.
:::

The $L^2$ error of a partial sum is an integral of a trigonometric polynomial squared, and Parseval predicts it
from the omitted coefficients. The second example computes it for $S_9$ and explains the number $0.2538$.

::: {#exm-fs-sage-l2-error}
#### The $L^2$ error of $S_9$

By Parseval applied to $f - S_9 f$, whose coefficients are those of $f$ for odd $n > 9$ and zero otherwise,
$\int_{-\pi}^\pi(f - S_9 f)^2 = \pi\sum_{\text{odd } n > 9}\frac{16}{\pi^2n^2} = 2\pi - \pi\sum_{\text{odd } n \leq
9}\frac{16}{\pi^2n^2} = 0.2538\ldots$. Integrating $(1 - S_9f)^2$ over $(0, \pi)$ directly and doubling gives the
same exact expression, since by @eq-mode-orthogonality the cross terms between different harmonics vanish.
:::

The Gibbs constant is a limit, and evaluating the partial sum at its first maximum for a single large $N$ shows
how close the approach already is. The third example does this for $N = 199$ and compares the value with the
integral $\operatorname{Si}(\pi)$.

::: {#exm-fs-sage-gibbs}
#### The Gibbs constant at $N = 199$

At $N = 199$ the first maximum is near $x = \pi/200$, and $S_{199}(\pi/200) = \frac4\pi\sum_{\text{odd } n \leq
199}\sin(n\pi/200)/n = 1.1790\ldots$ is a Riemann sum with $100$ points for $\frac2\pi\int_0^\pi\frac{\sin t}{t}dt
= \frac2\pi\operatorname{Si}(\pi) = 1.17897974\ldots$, the Gibbs constant. The two agree to $10^{-3}$; the
difference, about $10^{-5}$, is the Riemann-sum error of @exr-fs-gibbs.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The triangle wave is the integral of the square wave, and its coefficients decay one power faster, so its partial
sums converge uniformly and without overshoot. The first exercise computes them in Sage and watches the maximal
error decrease.

::: {#exr-fs-triangle-wave}
#### The triangle wave

Compute the Fourier coefficients of the triangle wave $f(x) = \pi/2 - |x|$ on $(-\pi, \pi)$ with Sage, plot or
tabulate the maximal error $\max_x|f - S_N f|$ for $N = 1, 3, 9, 29$, and relate the decay to
@exr-fs-coefficients-decay.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$f = \frac4\pi\sum_k\frac{\cos(2k + 1)x}{(2k + 1)^2}$ (shift the series of $|x|$), and the maximal error is
bounded by the tail $\frac4\pi\sum_{2k + 1 > N}(2k + 1)^{-2} \approx \frac{2}{\pi N}$, so it decreases like $1/N$
with no overshoot, as the $1/n^2$ decay of a continuous piecewise $C^1$ function predicts:

{{< sage exr-fs-triangle-wave >}}
:::

For a function with a jump the $L^2$ error decreases only like $1/N$, and Parseval gives the precise constant.
The second exercise tabulates the exact errors for the square wave in Sage and compares them with the tail
formula.

::: {#exr-fs-l2-error}
#### $L^2$ errors of the square wave

Compute $\int_{-\pi}^\pi(f - S_N f)^2\,dx$ for the square wave and $N = 1, 3, 9, 29$ in two ways, by exact
integration and by Parseval's tail sum, and show that the error behaves like $8/(\pi N)$ for large $N$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The tail is $\frac{16}{\pi}\sum_{\text{odd } n > N}n^{-2} \approx \frac{16}{\pi}\cdot\frac{1}{2N} = \frac{8}{\pi
N}$, comparing the sum over odd $n$ with half the integral $\int_N^\infty dn/n^2$; the exact and the tail values
agree, and $N$ times the error approaches $8/\pi = 2.546$:

{{< sage exr-fs-l2-error >}}
:::

A function on $[0, \pi]$ can be expanded in sines alone or in cosines alone, by extending it to $(-\pi, \pi)$ as
an odd or an even function. The third exercise connects these half-range expansions with the Dirichlet modes of
@sec-sturm-liouville and explains which one converges better.

::: {#exr-fs-half-range}
#### Half-range expansions

Show that a function $f$ on $[0, \pi]$ has a sine series $\sum b_n\sin nx$ with $b_n = \frac2\pi\int_0^\pi f\sin
nx$ and a cosine series $\frac{a_0}{2} + \sum a_n\cos nx$ with $a_n = \frac2\pi\int_0^\pi f\cos nx$, identify
them with the expansions in the Dirichlet and Neumann eigenfunctions of $-d^2/dx^2$ on $[0, \pi]$, and explain
why the cosine series of $f(x) = x$ converges uniformly while the sine series does not.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The odd extension $f_o(-x) = -f(x)$ has $a_n = 0$ and $b_n = \frac1\pi\int_{-\pi}^\pi f_o\sin nx =
\frac2\pi\int_0^\pi f\sin nx$; the even extension has $b_n = 0$ and $a_n = \frac2\pi\int_0^\pi f\cos nx$. The
sines $\sin nx$ are the eigenfunctions of $-d^2/dx^2$ with $u(0) = u(\pi) = 0$ and the cosines those with $u'(0)
= u'(\pi) = 0$ (@thm-sturm-liouville, @exr-slt-fourier-sine), so the half-range series are the eigenfunction
expansions of the two boundary value problems. The odd extension of $f(x) = x$ is the sawtooth, discontinuous at
$\pm\pi$, with coefficients $2(-1)^{n+1}/n$ and non-uniform convergence; the even extension is $|x|$, continuous,
with coefficients $O(1/n^2)$ and uniform convergence (@exm-fs-convergence-abs). A function vanishing at both ends,
such as $\sin x$ or $x(\pi - x)$, has an odd extension that is continuous, and then the sine series converges
uniformly too.
:::

## The Fourier transform {#sec-fourier-transform}

A function on the whole line has no period, and the discrete harmonics $e^{inx}$ are replaced by the continuum of
plane waves $e^{ikx}$ with the sum over $n$ replaced by an integral over $k$. This section defines the transform
and its inverse, computes it for the box, the two-sided exponential and the Gaussian, proves the convolution
theorem, states Plancherel's theorem and the uncertainty inequality, and ends with a proposition that collects
the explicit transforms; the figure shows the trade-off between the width of a Gaussian and the width of
its transform.

![Gaussians $e^{-x^2/2\sigma^2}$ of width $\sigma = \tfrac12, 1, 2$ (left) and their Fourier transforms
$\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}\,e^{-\sigma^2k^2/2}$ (right): the narrower the function, the wider its transform, with
$\Delta x\,\Delta k = \tfrac12$ exactly. Generated by
`figures/fourier_gaussian.sage`.](figures/fourier_gaussian.svg){#fig-fourier-gaussian width=95%}

{{< interactive fourier_gaussian 460 >}}

### The transform

The Fourier transform of an integrable function is its inner product with every plane wave at once, a function of
the wave number $k$. The definition fixes the normalisation used throughout the book, lists the rules that make
the transform computable, and records the heuristic that it is a Fourier series whose period has gone to
infinity.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-fourier-transform}
#### Fourier transform

For $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{C}$ with $\int_{-\infty}^\infty|f| < \infty$ (**absolutely integrable**), the
**Fourier transform** is
$$
\hat f(k) = \int_{-\infty}^\infty f(x)\,e^{-ikx}\,dx, \qquad k \in \mathbb{R},
$$ {#eq-fourier-transform}
a bounded continuous function with $|\hat f(k)| \leq \int|f|$ and $\hat f(k) \to 0$ as $|k| \to \infty$
(Riemann-Lebesgue). It obeys the **translation rule** $\widehat{f(x - a)} = e^{-ika}\hat f(k)$, the **modulation
rule** $\widehat{e^{iax}f} = \hat f(k - a)$, the **scaling rule** $\widehat{f(\lambda x)} = \hat
f(k/\lambda)/|\lambda|$, the **derivative rule** $\widehat{f'} = ik\hat f$ when $f$ is $C^1$ with $f, f'$
integrable, and the **multiplication rule** $\widehat{xf} = i\,\hat f\,'$ when $xf$ is integrable; a **Schwartz
function**, smooth with all derivatives decaying faster than any power, has a Schwartz transform. Heuristically,
$f$ on $[-L, L]$ has the series $\sum_n c_n e^{i\pi nx/L}$ with $2Lc_n = \hat f(\pi n/L)$, and as $L \to \infty$
the sum over the wave numbers $k_n = \pi n/L$ spaced by $\pi/L$ becomes $\frac{1}{2\pi}\int\hat f(k)e^{ikx}dk$,
which is the inversion formula of @thm-fourier-inversion.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The box function is the simplest integrable function, and its transform is the first appearance of the sinc
function. The first example computes it and reads off the slow decay that goes with the jumps.

::: {#exm-ft-box}
#### The box

For the **box** $\chi_a = 1$ on $[-a, a]$ and $0$ outside, $\hat\chi_a(k) = \int_{-a}^a e^{-ikx}dx = \frac{e^{-ika} -
e^{ika}}{-ik} = \frac{2\sin ak}{k}$ (@prp-fourier-transform-values), with $\hat\chi_a(0) = 2a$ the area of the
box. The transform decays only like $1/|k|$ and is not absolutely integrable, the counterpart of the $1/n$
decay of the square wave's coefficients: a jump in $f$ costs a power of $k$ in $\hat f$.
:::

The two-sided exponential is continuous with a kink, and its transform is the Lorentzian, decaying one power
faster than the sinc. The second example integrates the two half-lines separately and adds the results.

::: {#exm-ft-exponential}
#### The two-sided exponential

For $f(x) = e^{-a|x|}$ with $a > 0$, $\hat f(k) = \int_0^\infty e^{-(a + ik)x}dx + \int_{-\infty}^0 e^{(a -
ik)x}dx = \frac{1}{a + ik} + \frac{1}{a - ik} = \frac{2a}{a^2 + k^2}$ (@prp-fourier-transform-values), the *
*Lorentzian**, decaying like $1/k^2$ because $f$ is continuous with a jump in $f'$. It is integrable, so the
inversion formula applies at every point (@exm-ft-inversion-lorentzian).
:::

The Gaussian is the central example of the chapter: its transform is again a Gaussian, with the inverse width.
The third example derives this by completing the square and shifting the contour, and notes the special role of
$\sigma = 1$.

::: {#exm-ft-gaussian}
#### The Gaussian

For $g_\sigma(x) = e^{-x^2/2\sigma^2}$, completing the square gives $-\frac{x^2}{2\sigma^2} - ikx = -
\frac{(x + ik\sigma^2)^2}{2\sigma^2} - \frac{\sigma^2k^2}{2}$, so
$$
\hat g_\sigma(k) = e^{-\sigma^2k^2/2}\int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-(x + ik\sigma^2)^2/2\sigma^2}dx =
\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}\,e^{-\sigma^2k^2/2},
$$ {#eq-gaussian-transform}
where the shifted integral equals the Gaussian integral $\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}$ of @sec-riemann-integral because the
integrand is entire and the horizontal line $\operatorname{Im} x = -k\sigma^2$ can be moved to the real axis
(@thm-cauchy, @exr-ca-gaussian-fourier). A Gaussian of width $\sigma$ transforms to a Gaussian of width
$1/\sigma$ (@fig-fourier-gaussian), and for $\sigma = 1$ the function reproduces itself up to the factor
$\sqrt{2\pi}$: $e^{-x^2/2}$ is an eigenfunction of the transform (@exr-ft-hermite-eigen).
:::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The five rules of the definition are each a one-line substitution or integration by parts, and knowing them is
what makes transforms computable without integrating. The first exercise asks for the derivations, with
attention to the hypotheses on the derivative rule.

::: {#exr-ft-rules}
#### The transform rules

Prove the translation, modulation, scaling, derivative and multiplication rules of @def-fourier-transform, and
use them to find the transforms of $e^{-(x - 3)^2/2}$, $e^{-2|x|}\cos 5x$ and $x e^{-x^2/2}$ from the examples.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Substituting $y = x - a$, $\int f(x - a)e^{-ikx}dx = e^{-ika}\int f(y)e^{-iky}dy$; $\int e^{iax}f e^{-ikx} = \hat
f(k - a)$ directly; $y = \lambda x$ gives $\int f(\lambda x)e^{-ikx}dx = \frac{1}{|\lambda|}\int
f(y)e^{-i(k/\lambda)y}dy$, the absolute value from the reversed limits when $\lambda < 0$. Integrating by parts,
$\int f'e^{-ikx} = [fe^{-ikx}]_{-\infty}^\infty + ik\int fe^{-ikx} = ik\hat f$, the boundary term vanishing since
an integrable $C^1$ function with integrable derivative tends to $0$ at $\pm\infty$ ($f(x) = f(0) + \int_0^x f'$
has a limit, which must be $0$). Differentiating under the integral (@thm-differentiation-under-integral,
dominated by $|xf|$), $\hat f\,'(k) = \int(-ix)fe^{-ikx} = -i\,\widehat{xf}$. Then $\widehat{e^{-(x -
3)^2/2}} = e^{-3ik}\sqrt{2\pi}e^{-k^2/2}$; $e^{-2|x|}\cos 5x = \tfrac12(e^{5ix} + e^{-5ix})e^{-2|x|}$ transforms to
$\frac{2}{4 + (k - 5)^2} + \frac{2}{4 + (k + 5)^2}$; and $\widehat{xe^{-x^2/2}} = i\frac{d}{dk}\sqrt{2\pi}e^{-k^2/2}
= -ik\sqrt{2\pi}e^{-k^2/2}$.
:::

A function supported on a half-line has a transform that extends to the complex plane on one side, a property
the next chapters' Green's functions depend on. The second exercise computes the transform of the one-sided
exponential and locates its pole, with Sage handling the integral.

::: {#exr-ft-one-sided}
#### The one-sided exponential

Compute the transform of $f(x) = \theta(x)e^{-ax}$ ($a > 0$, $\theta$ the step function), show that it extends
to a holomorphic function of $k$ in the half-plane $\operatorname{Im} k < a$, which contains the whole lower
half-plane, with a pole at $k = ia$, and check the transform and its real and imaginary parts with Sage.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\hat f(k) = \int_0^\infty e^{-(a + ik)x}dx = \frac{1}{a + ik} = \frac{a - ik}{a^2 + k^2}$, whose real part is
half the Lorentzian of @exm-ft-exponential and whose imaginary part $-k/(a^2 + k^2)$ is odd. The integral
converges whenever $\operatorname{Re}(a + ik) = a - \operatorname{Im} k > 0$, and the result $1/(a + ik)$ is
holomorphic there, its only pole $k = ia$ lying on the boundary line $\operatorname{Im} k = a$ of the region; in
general a function vanishing for $x < 0$ has a transform holomorphic in the lower half-plane $\operatorname{Im} k
< 0$, the origin of the retarded prescription of @sec-greens-functions:

{{< sage exr-ft-one-sided >}}
:::

The Gaussian transform can be obtained without any contour shifting, by turning the derivative and
multiplication rules into a differential equation for $\hat g$. The third exercise asks for this derivation,
which generalises to every function satisfying a linear differential equation with polynomial coefficients.

::: {#exr-ft-gaussian-ode}
#### The Gaussian transform by a differential equation

Show that $g = e^{-x^2/2\sigma^2}$ satisfies $\sigma^2g' + xg = 0$, transform this equation using the rules to
obtain $\hat g\,' = -\sigma^2k\hat g$, and solve it to recover @eq-gaussian-transform; then explain why the same
method gives the transform of $e^{-ax^2}$ for complex $a$ with $\operatorname{Re} a > 0$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$g' = -(x/\sigma^2)g$ is the equation. Transforming, $\sigma^2\,ik\hat g + i\hat g\,' = 0$, that is, $\hat g\,' = -
\sigma^2k\hat g$, whose solution is $\hat g(k) = \hat g(0)e^{-\sigma^2k^2/2}$ with $\hat g(0) = \int g =
\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}$ the Gaussian integral. For $e^{-ax^2}$ the equation is $g' = -2axg$, giving $\hat g(k) = \hat
g(0)e^{-k^2/4a}$ with $\hat g(0) = \int e^{-ax^2}dx = \sqrt{\pi/a}$, the principal branch of the root; this holds
for $\operatorname{Re} a > 0$ because both sides are holomorphic in $a$ there and agree for real $a > 0$
(@sec-analytic-continuation), and it is the form used for the free propagator in the chapters on quantum
mechanics.
:::

### Inversion

A function is recovered from its transform by the inverse integral, with the factor $1/2\pi$ placed in the inverse
in this book. The theorem states the inversion formula under a hypothesis that covers the examples, sketches the
proof by Gaussian regularisation, and records the duality that the transform of a transform is the reflected
function.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#thm-fourier-inversion}
#### Fourier inversion

If $f$ and $\hat f$ are both absolutely integrable and $f$ is continuous, then
$$
f(x) = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\infty}^\infty\hat f(k)\,e^{ikx}\,dk
$$ {#eq-fourier-inversion}
for every $x$; if $f$ is only piecewise $C^1$ the right side converges, as $\lim_{L \to \infty}\int_{-L}^L$, to
$\tfrac12(f(x^+) + f(x^-))$. In particular $\hat{\hat f}(x) = 2\pi f(-x)$ (**duality**). *Argument.* Insert the
convergence factor $e^{-\varepsilon k^2/2}$: by Fubini (@sec-multiple-integrals) and @eq-gaussian-transform,
$\frac{1}{2\pi}\int\hat f(k)e^{-\varepsilon k^2/2}e^{ikx}dk = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int f(y)\int e^{-\varepsilon
k^2/2}e^{ik(x - y)}dk\,dy = \int f(y)\frac{e^{-(x - y)^2/2\varepsilon}}{\sqrt{2\pi\varepsilon}}dy$, the
convolution of $f$ with a Gaussian of unit integral and width $\sqrt\varepsilon$, which tends to $f(x)$ as
$\varepsilon \to 0$ at points of continuity (@exr-ft-inversion-gaussian); the left side tends to
$\frac{1}{2\pi}\int\hat f e^{ikx}$ by dominated convergence since $\hat f$ is integrable. The piecewise $C^1$ case
uses the kernel $\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-L}^Le^{ik(x - y)}dk = \frac{\sin L(x - y)}{\pi(x - y)}$ in place of the
Gaussian, as in Dirichlet's theorem.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
Inverting the Lorentzian is a residue computation, and it is the first time the two halves of complex analysis,
contour integration and the Fourier transform, meet. The first example carries it out with the semicircle closed
in the half-plane where the exponential decays.

::: {#exm-ft-inversion-lorentzian}
#### Inverting the Lorentzian by residues

$\frac{1}{2\pi}\int\frac{2a}{a^2 + k^2}e^{ikx}dk$ for $x > 0$: close the contour in the upper half-plane, where
$|e^{ikx}| = e^{-x\operatorname{Im}k}$ decays, enclosing the pole at $k = ia$ with residue $\frac{2a\,e^{-ax}}{2ia}
= \frac{e^{-ax}}{i}$; the residue theorem (@thm-residue) gives $\frac{1}{2\pi}\cdot2\pi i\cdot\frac{e^{-ax}}{i} =
e^{-ax}$. For $x < 0$ close below and obtain $e^{ax}$, so the inverse transform is $e^{-a|x|}$, as
@exm-ft-exponential requires (@exr-ft-lorentzian-inverse).
:::

The box has a transform that is not integrable, and inversion holds only in the symmetric-limit sense of the
theorem, with the midpoint value at the jumps. The second example recovers the box from the sinc function and
reads off the Dirichlet integral.

::: {#exm-ft-inversion-box}
#### Inverting the sinc

$\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-L}^L\frac{2\sin ak}{k}e^{ikx}dk = \frac{1}{\pi}\int_{-L}^L\frac{\sin ak\cos kx}{k}dk$ (the
sine part is odd) $= \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-L}^L\frac{\sin(a + x)k + \sin(a - x)k}{k}dk \to \frac{1}{2\pi}\bigl[\pi
\operatorname{sgn}(a + x) + \pi\operatorname{sgn}(a - x)\bigr]$ by the Dirichlet integral
$\int_{-\infty}^\infty\frac{\sin ck}{k}dk = \pi\operatorname{sgn} c$ (@prp-distribution-identities). This is $1$
for $|x| < a$, $0$ for $|x| > a$ and $\tfrac12$ at $x = \pm a$: the box with the midpoint rule at its jumps.
:::

Applying the transform twice returns the reflected function times $2\pi$, so the transform of a sinc is a box
and the transform of a Lorentzian is an exponential. The third example lists these dual pairs, which are the
way the non-integrable transforms are used in practice.

::: {#exm-ft-duality}
#### Dual pairs

From $\hat{\hat f}(x) = 2\pi f(-x)$ and the even functions of the examples: $\widehat{\sin ax/x} = \pi\chi_a(k)$
(the transform of the sinc is a box, of height $\pi$ on $[-a, a]$), $\widehat{1/(a^2 + x^2)} = \frac\pi a
e^{-a|k|}$, and $\widehat{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}e^{-\sigma^2x^2/2}} = 2\pi e^{-k^2/2\sigma^2}$, consistent with
@eq-gaussian-transform at width $1/\sigma$. The first pair needs the extended sense of the transform, since
$\sin ax/x$ is not absolutely integrable; @sec-distributions makes it rigorous.
:::

The step in the inversion argument that needs real analysis is the convergence of the Gaussian regularisation,
an approximate identity. The second exercise proves it, which is the same estimate that makes the delta function
a limit of Gaussians in @sec-distributions.

::: {#exr-ft-inversion-gaussian}
#### Gaussian regularisation

Let $G_\varepsilon(x) = e^{-x^2/2\varepsilon}/\sqrt{2\pi\varepsilon}$. Show that $\int G_\varepsilon = 1$, that for
every $\delta > 0$, $\int_{|y| > \delta}G_\varepsilon(y)\,dy \to 0$ as $\varepsilon \to 0$, and that $\int
f(x - y)G_\varepsilon(y)\,dy \to f(x)$ for every bounded $f$ continuous at $x$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\int G_\varepsilon = 1$ is the Gaussian integral; substituting $y = \sqrt\varepsilon\,u$, $\int_{|y| >
\delta}G_\varepsilon = \int_{|u| > \delta/\sqrt\varepsilon}e^{-u^2/2}du/\sqrt{2\pi} \to 0$ as the lower limit
goes to infinity. Then $\int f(x - y)G_\varepsilon(y)dy - f(x) = \int[f(x - y) - f(x)]G_\varepsilon(y)dy$; split
at $|y| = \delta$, where $\delta$ is chosen so that $|f(x - y) - f(x)| < \eta$ for $|y| < \delta$: the inner part
is at most $\eta$ and the outer part at most $2\sup|f|\int_{|y| > \delta}G_\varepsilon \to 0$. So the limit
superior is at most $\eta$ for every $\eta > 0$.
:::

The duality $\hat{\hat f} = 2\pi f(-x)$ means that the transform applied four times is $(2\pi)^2$ times the
identity, so its eigenvalues are the four fourth roots of $(2\pi)^2$. The third exercise identifies the first two
eigenfunctions, the Gaussian and the Gaussian times $x$, which begin the Hermite functions.

::: {#exr-ft-hermite-eigen}
#### Eigenfunctions of the transform

Show from the duality that the only possible eigenvalues of $f \mapsto \hat f$ are $\pm\sqrt{2\pi}$ and
$\pm i\sqrt{2\pi}$, verify with Sage that $e^{-x^2/2}$ and $xe^{-x^2/2}$ are eigenfunctions with eigenvalues
$\sqrt{2\pi}$ and $-i\sqrt{2\pi}$, and find the eigenvalue of $(2x^2 - 1)e^{-x^2/2}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
If $\hat f = \lambda f$ then $\hat{\hat f} = \lambda^2 f$ and $2\pi f(-x) = \lambda^2 f(x)$; applying this twice,
$(2\pi)^2 f = \lambda^4 f$, so $\lambda^4 = (2\pi)^2$. The Gaussian is even with $\lambda = \sqrt{2\pi}$;
$xe^{-x^2/2}$ is odd and transforms to $-ik\sqrt{2\pi}e^{-k^2/2}$ by the multiplication rule; $(2x^2 -
1)e^{-x^2/2}$ transforms to $-\sqrt{2\pi}(2k^2 - 1)e^{-k^2/2}$, eigenvalue $-\sqrt{2\pi}$. These are the first three
Hermite functions $H_n(x)e^{-x^2/2}$, with eigenvalues $(-i)^n\sqrt{2\pi}$, the eigenfunctions of the harmonic
oscillator of the quantum-mechanics chapters:

{{< sage exr-ft-hermite-eigen >}}
:::

### Convolution

Multiplying transforms corresponds to an operation on the functions themselves, the convolution, which is also
how a function is smoothed or averaged. The definition introduces it, states the convolution theorem in both
directions, and names the smoothing property that makes approximate identities work.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-convolution}
#### Convolution

The **convolution** of two integrable functions is
$$
(f * g)(x) = \int_{-\infty}^\infty f(x - y)\,g(y)\,dy = \int_{-\infty}^\infty f(y)\,g(x - y)\,dy,
$$
commutative and associative, integrable with $\int|f * g| \leq \int|f|\int|g|$. The **convolution theorem** states
$$
\widehat{f * g} = \hat f\,\hat g, \qquad \widehat{fg} = \frac{1}{2\pi}\,\hat f * \hat g,
$$ {#eq-convolution-theorem}
the first for integrable $f, g$ and the second when $f, g$ and their transforms are integrable. Convolution
**smooths**: $f * g$ is as differentiable as the better of $f$ and $g$, with $(f * g)' = f' * g = f * g'$; and
convolving with a family of non-negative functions of unit integral concentrating at $0$ (an **approximate
identity**, such as the Gaussians of @exr-ft-inversion-gaussian) returns $f$ in the limit.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
Convolving a box with itself produces a triangle, and the convolution theorem predicts that the sinc function
squares. The first example computes the convolution directly and compares the two transforms, which agree
exactly.

::: {#exm-ft-box-box}
#### Box times box is a triangle

$(\chi_a * \chi_a)(x) = \int\chi_a(x - y)\chi_a(y)\,dy$ is the length of $[-a, a] \cap [x - a, x + a]$, which is
$2a - |x|$ for $|x| \leq 2a$ and $0$ otherwise: the **triangle** $\Lambda_a$. By @eq-convolution-theorem its
transform is $\hat\chi_a^2 = 4\sin^2 ak/k^2$, which direct integration confirms (@prp-fourier-transform-values);
the triangle is continuous with kinks, and its transform decays like $1/k^2$, one power better than the box.
:::

Gaussians are closed under convolution, with the variances adding, which is the fact behind the central limit
theorem and the heat kernel's semigroup property. The second example obtains it from the convolution theorem in
one line.

::: {#exm-ft-gaussian-gaussian}
#### Gaussians convolve to Gaussians

With $g_\sigma = e^{-x^2/2\sigma^2}$, $\widehat{g_\sigma * g_\tau} = \hat g_\sigma\hat g_\tau =
2\pi\sigma\tau\,e^{-(\sigma^2 + \tau^2)k^2/2}$, which by @eq-gaussian-transform is the transform of
$\frac{\sigma\tau\sqrt{2\pi}}{\sqrt{\sigma^2 + \tau^2}}g_{\sqrt{\sigma^2 + \tau^2}}$: the widths add in
quadrature. For the normalised Gaussians $G_\varepsilon$ of @exr-ft-inversion-gaussian this reads $G_\varepsilon *
G_\eta = G_{\varepsilon + \eta}$, the semigroup property of the heat kernel (@def-heat-equation).
:::

A linear differential equation with constant coefficients becomes an algebraic equation after the transform, and
its solution is a convolution with the inverse transform of the algebraic factor. The third example does this for
the heat equation and identifies the heat kernel as a Gaussian.

::: {#exm-ft-convolution-heat}
#### The heat equation by the transform

Transforming $u_t = \kappa u_{xx}$ in $x$ turns it into $\hat u_t = -\kappa k^2\hat u$ by the derivative rule, so
$\hat u(t, k) = e^{-\kappa k^2t}\hat u_0(k)$, and by the convolution theorem $u(t, \cdot) = K_t * u_0$ with $K_t$
the inverse transform of $e^{-\kappa k^2t}$, which by @eq-gaussian-transform with $\sigma^2 = 2\kappa t$ is
$K_t(x) = \frac{e^{-x^2/4\kappa t}}{\sqrt{4\pi\kappa t}}$, the heat kernel of @def-heat-equation
(@exr-ft-heat-kernel). The smoothing of the convolution is the smoothing of heat flow.
:::

The transform of the triangle can be computed directly, by integrating over its two linear pieces, and the result
must be the square of the sinc. The first exercise does this in Sage and uses the result to evaluate the
convolution at a point.

::: {#exr-ft-triangle}
#### The triangle's transform

Compute $\hat\Lambda_a(k)$ directly from the two linear pieces of the triangle with Sage, verify that it equals
$(2\sin ak/k)^2$, and evaluate $(\chi_1 * \chi_1)(\tfrac12)$ both from the triangle formula and from the
convolution integral.

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\int_{-2a}^0(2a + x)e^{-ikx}dx + \int_0^{2a}(2a - x)e^{-ikx}dx = \frac{2 - 2\cos 2ak}{k^2} = \frac{4\sin^2
ak}{k^2}$, and $(\chi_1 * \chi_1)(\tfrac12) = 2 - \tfrac12 = \tfrac32$, the length of $[-1, 1] \cap [-\tfrac12,
\tfrac32]$:

{{< sage exr-ft-triangle >}}
:::

The convolution theorem is an exchange of the order of integration followed by the translation rule, and the
second form follows from the first by duality. The second exercise asks for both derivations and for the
smoothing property.

::: {#exr-ft-convolution-theorem}
#### Proof of the convolution theorem

Prove $\widehat{f * g} = \hat f\hat g$ for integrable $f, g$ by Fubini's theorem, deduce $\widehat{fg} =
\frac{1}{2\pi}\hat f * \hat g$ from inversion and duality, and show that $(f * g)' = f' * g$ when $f$ is $C^1$
with $f'$ integrable.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\int(f * g)(x)e^{-ikx}dx = \int\int f(x - y)g(y)e^{-ikx}dy\,dx = \int g(y)\Bigl[\int f(x - y)e^{-ikx}dx\Bigr]dy =
\int g(y)e^{-iky}\hat f(k)dy = \hat f(k)\hat g(k)$, the exchange justified by $\int\int|f(x - y)||g(y)| =
\int|f|\int|g| < \infty$ (@sec-multiple-integrals) and the inner integral by the translation rule. For the
second, write $f = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int\hat f(p)e^{ipx}dp$; then $\widehat{fg}(k) = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int\hat
f(p)\widehat{e^{ipx}g}(k)dp = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int\hat f(p)\hat g(k - p)dp$ by the modulation rule. Finally
$\frac{d}{dx}\int f(x - y)g(y)dy = \int f'(x - y)g(y)dy$ by differentiation under the integral
(@thm-differentiation-under-integral), dominated by $\sup|f'|\,|g|$ when $f'$ is bounded, or by an approximation
argument in general.
:::

#### The heat kernel by inverse transform

Compute the inverse transform of $e^{-\kappa k^2t}$ with Sage, verify that it solves $u_t = \kappa u_{xx}$ and
has unit integral, and solve the heat equation with the initial profile $u_0 = e^{-x^2/2}$ by the convolution

solution is $\sqrt{2\pi}e^{-(1 + 2\kappa t)k^2/2}$, whose inverse is $u(t, x) = (1 + 2\kappa t)^{-1/2}e^{-x^2/2(1 +
2\kappa t)}$: a Gaussian whose variance grows linearly in time, as @exm-ft-gaussian-gaussian predicts:

{{< sage exr-ft-heat-kernel >}}

### Plancherel's theorem

Parseval's identity for the line says that the transform preserves the squared integral, up to the factor
$2\pi$ of the normalisation. The theorem states it with the polarised form, derives it from the convolution
theorem and inversion, and records the extension that makes the transform a unitary map of the square-integrable
functions.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#thm-plancherel}
#### Plancherel's theorem

If $f$ is absolutely and square integrable, then $\hat f$ is square integrable and
$$
\int_{-\infty}^\infty|f(x)|^2\,dx = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\infty}^\infty|\hat f(k)|^2\,dk, \qquad
\int\bar f g\,dx = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int\bar{\hat f}\hat g\,dk .
$$ {#eq-plancherel}
The map $f \mapsto \hat f/\sqrt{2\pi}$ extends to a unitary operator on the square-integrable functions on
$\mathbb{R}$ (the space $L^2$ of the next chapter), whose inverse is $f \mapsto \sqrt{2\pi}\,\check f$ with
$\check f(x) = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int f(k)e^{ikx}dk$; the transform of a square-integrable $f$ that is not
integrable is defined as the $L^2$ limit of the transforms of its truncations $f\chi_L$. *Argument.* Let $h(y) =
\overline{f(-y)}$, so that $\hat h = \bar{\hat f}$. Then $(f * h)(0) = \int f(-y)\overline{f(-y)}dy = \int|f|^2$,
while $\widehat{f * h} = |\hat f|^2$, and inversion at $x = 0$ gives $(f * h)(0) = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int|\hat f|^2$
(@exr-ft-plancherel-proof); the polarised form follows from $f + g$ and $f + ig$, and the extension to $L^2$
by density.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
Plancherel's theorem evaluates integrals of squared transforms that would otherwise need contour integration.
The first example takes the box and obtains the integral of $\sin^2x/x^2$, one of the items of
@prp-fourier-transform-values.

::: {#exm-ft-plancherel-box}
#### $\int\sin^2 x/x^2 = \pi$

For the box $\chi_a$, $\int|\chi_a|^2 = 2a$ and $\hat\chi_a = 2\sin ak/k$, so @eq-plancherel gives
$\frac{1}{2\pi}\int\frac{4\sin^2 ak}{k^2}dk = 2a$ (@prp-fourier-transform-values), that is,
$\int_{-\infty}^\infty\frac{\sin^2 ak}{k^2}dk = \pi a$, and with $a = 1$, $\int\frac{\sin^2x}{x^2}dx = \pi$, the
same value as the Dirichlet integral $\int\frac{\sin x}{x}dx$ (@exr-ft-sinc-integrals).
:::

For the two-sided exponential the theorem gives the integral of the squared Lorentzian, a standard residue
integral obtained for free. The second example records it and the consistency of the Gaussian case.

::: {#exm-ft-plancherel-lorentzian}
#### The squared Lorentzian

$\int e^{-2a|x|}dx = 1/a$ and $\hat f = 2a/(a^2 + k^2)$, so $\frac{1}{2\pi}\int\frac{4a^2}{(a^2 + k^2)^2}dk =
\frac1a$, that is, $\int\frac{dk}{(a^2 + k^2)^2} = \frac{\pi}{2a^3}$, which the residue theorem at the double pole
$k = ia$ confirms. For the Gaussian, $\int e^{-x^2/\sigma^2} = \sigma\sqrt\pi$ and $\frac{1}{2\pi}\int
2\pi\sigma^2e^{-\sigma^2k^2} = \sigma^2\cdot\frac{\sqrt\pi}{\sigma} = \sigma\sqrt\pi$: consistent.
:::

The theorem is also the statement that the transform preserves inner products, and the Hermite functions of
@exr-ft-hermite-eigen show it in action: orthogonal eigenfunctions with different eigenvalues. The third example
makes this explicit and notes what unitarity says about the eigenvalues.

::: {#exm-ft-plancherel-hermite}
#### Orthogonality of the Hermite functions

$e^{-x^2/2}$ and $xe^{-x^2/2}$ are orthogonal, $\int xe^{-x^2}dx = 0$ by oddness, and so are their transforms
$\sqrt{2\pi}e^{-k^2/2}$ and $-ik\sqrt{2\pi}e^{-k^2/2}$, as the polarised identity requires. More generally, since
$f \mapsto \hat f/\sqrt{2\pi}$ is unitary, its eigenvalues $\lambda/\sqrt{2\pi} \in \{1, -i, -1, i\}$ have modulus
$1$, which is what @exr-ft-hermite-eigen found, and eigenfunctions with distinct eigenvalues are automatically
orthogonal, as for every unitary or self-adjoint operator (@sec-linear-algebra).
:::

The integrals of powers of the sinc function come from Plancherel applied to the box and the triangle, and Sage
can confirm them directly. The first exercise asks for $\int\sin^2x/x^2$ and $\int\sin^4x/x^4$ by this route.

::: {#exr-ft-sinc-integrals}
#### Integrals of powers of the sinc

Use Plancherel's theorem for the box and for the triangle to evaluate $\int_{-\infty}^\infty\frac{\sin^2x}{x^2}dx$
and $\int_{-\infty}^\infty\frac{\sin^4x}{x^4}dx$, and check both with Sage.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
For $\chi_1$: $2 = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int\frac{4\sin^2k}{k^2}dk$, so the first integral is $\pi$. For $\Lambda_1$ with
$\hat\Lambda_1 = 4\sin^2k/k^2$: $\int\Lambda_1^2 = 2\int_0^2(2 - x)^2dx = \frac{16}{3}$, so
$\frac{1}{2\pi}\int\frac{16\sin^4k}{k^4}dk = \frac{16}{3}$ and the second integral is $\frac{2\pi}{3}$:

{{< sage exr-ft-sinc-integrals >}}
:::

The argument sketched in the theorem has one step to check, the transform of the reflected conjugate, and the
polarisation that follows. The second exercise asks for these details and for the inner-product form applied to
two explicit functions.

::: {#exr-ft-plancherel-proof}
#### Completing the proof of Plancherel

Show that $h(y) = \overline{f(-y)}$ has $\hat h = \bar{\hat f}$, complete the argument of @thm-plancherel, derive
the polarised identity from the quadratic one, and apply it to $f = \chi_1$ and $g = e^{-|x|}$ to evaluate
$\int_{-\infty}^\infty\frac{\sin k}{k}\frac{dk}{1 + k^2}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\hat h(k) = \int\overline{f(-y)}e^{-iky}dy = \overline{\int f(-y)e^{iky}dy} = \overline{\int f(u)e^{-iku}du} =
\overline{\hat f(k)}$. Then $\widehat{f * h} = \hat f\hat h = |\hat f|^2$ is integrable when $\hat f$ is square
integrable, $f * h$ is continuous, and inversion at $0$ gives $\int|f|^2 = (f * h)(0) = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int|\hat
f|^2$. Polarisation: $\int\bar fg = \tfrac14\sum_{m=0}^3 i^m\int|f + i^mg|^2$ and the same for the transforms,
termwise equal. For $f = \chi_1$, $g = e^{-|x|}$: $\int\chi_1e^{-|x|} = 2(1 - e^{-1})$ and $\frac{1}{2\pi}\int\frac{2\sin
k}{k}\cdot\frac{2}{1 + k^2}dk$, so $\int\frac{\sin k}{k(1 + k^2)}dk = \pi(1 - e^{-1})$.
:::

Sampling a function on the integers relates its Fourier series to its Fourier transform, and the result, the
Poisson summation formula, is the bridge between the first two sections. The third exercise derives it and
applies it to the Gaussian, where it becomes the functional equation of a theta function.

::: {#exr-ft-poisson-summation}
#### Poisson summation

Show that for a Schwartz function $f$, $\sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}}f(x + 2\pi n) = \frac{1}{2\pi}\sum_{n \in
\mathbb{Z}}\hat f(n)e^{inx}$, hence $\sum_n f(2\pi n) = \frac{1}{2\pi}\sum_n\hat f(n)$; apply it to $f =
e^{-x^2/2\sigma^2}$ and check the resulting identity numerically with Sage.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$F(x) = \sum_n f(x + 2\pi n)$ is $2\pi$-periodic and smooth, with Fourier coefficients $c_m =
\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\sum_nf(x + 2\pi n)e^{-imx}dx = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\infty}^\infty f(y)e^{-imy}dy =
\frac{\hat f(m)}{2\pi}$, the pieces $[2\pi n, 2\pi(n + 1)]$ reassembling the line and $e^{-im2\pi n} = 1$. Its
Fourier series converges absolutely (@thm-fourier-convergence) since $\hat f$ is Schwartz, and $x = 0$ gives the
second form. For the Gaussian, $\sum_ne^{-2\pi^2n^2/\sigma^2} = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\sum_ne^{-\sigma^2n^2/2}$,
an identity between two rapidly convergent series that exchanges $\sigma$ and $2\pi/\sigma$:

{{< sage exr-ft-poisson-summation >}}
:::

### The uncertainty inequality

A function and its transform cannot both be concentrated: the product of their widths is bounded below, with the
Gaussian as the unique extremal case. The theorem defines the widths as standard deviations, states the bound,
and proves it with one integration by parts and the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#thm-uncertainty}
#### The uncertainty inequality

For a $C^1$ function $f$ with $f, xf, f'$ square integrable, define the **widths** $\Delta x$ and $\Delta k$ by
$(\Delta x)^2 = \int x^2|f|^2dx\big/\!\int|f|^2dx$ and $(\Delta k)^2 = \int k^2|\hat f|^2dk\big/\!\int|\hat
f|^2dk$ (the centred case; in general replace $x$ by $x - \bar x$ and $k$ by $k - \bar k$). Then
$$
\Delta x\,\Delta k \geq \tfrac12,
$$ {#eq-uncertainty}
with equality if and only if $f$ is a Gaussian $Ce^{-x^2/2\sigma^2}$ (times $e^{i\bar kx}$ in the uncentred case).
*Proof.* By Plancherel and the derivative rule, $\int k^2|\hat f|^2 = \int|\widehat{f'}|^2 = 2\pi\int|f'|^2$ and
$\int|\hat f|^2 = 2\pi\int|f|^2$, so $(\Delta k)^2 = \int|f'|^2/\int|f|^2$. Integrating by parts,
$\int|f|^2 = \int\frac{d}{dx}(x)|f|^2 = -\int x(\bar f f' + f\bar f') = -2\operatorname{Re}\int x\bar ff'$, the
boundary term vanishing since $x|f|^2 \to 0$; by Cauchy-Schwarz $\int|f|^2 \leq 2\bigl(\int x^2|f|^2\bigr)^{1/2}\bigl(\int|f'|^2\bigr)^{1/2}$,
which is @eq-uncertainty. Equality requires $f' = -cxf$ with $c > 0$ real, whose solutions are the Gaussians.
:::

The Gaussian saturates the inequality, and the two widths can be computed exactly from the Gaussian integral and
its second moment. The first example does this and obtains the value $\tfrac12$ recorded in
@prp-fourier-transform-values.

::: {#exm-ft-uncertainty-gaussian}
#### The Gaussian saturates the bound

For $g_\sigma = e^{-x^2/2\sigma^2}$, $|g_\sigma|^2 = e^{-x^2/\sigma^2}$ has second moment $\sigma^2/2$ relative to
its integral, so $\Delta x = \sigma/\sqrt2$; $|\hat g_\sigma|^2 = 2\pi\sigma^2e^{-\sigma^2k^2}$ gives $\Delta k =
1/(\sigma\sqrt2)$; and $\Delta x\,\Delta k = \tfrac12$ for every $\sigma$ (@prp-fourier-transform-values): the
trade-off of @fig-fourier-gaussian is exactly balanced.
:::

A function that is not Gaussian has a strictly larger product, and the two-sided exponential gives the first
explicit value. The second example computes it with the Lorentzian transform.

::: {#exm-ft-uncertainty-exponential}
#### The exponential

For $f = e^{-a|x|}$, $|f|^2 = e^{-2a|x|}$ has $\int|f|^2 = 1/a$ and $\int x^2|f|^2 = 1/(2a^3)$, so $(\Delta x)^2 =
1/2a^2$; with $|\hat f|^2 = 4a^2/(a^2 + k^2)^2$, $\int|\hat f|^2 = 2\pi/a$ and $\int k^2|\hat f|^2 = 2\pi a$, so
$(\Delta k)^2 = a^2$ and $\Delta x\,\Delta k = 1/\sqrt2 > \tfrac12$ (@prp-fourier-transform-values). The kink at
$0$ costs the extra spread in $k$.
:::

A function with a jump has infinite width in $k$, because its transform decays too slowly for the second moment
to exist. The third example shows this for the box and relates it to the hypotheses of the theorem.

::: {#exm-ft-uncertainty-box}
#### The box has infinite $\Delta k$

For $\chi_a$, $\int k^2|\hat\chi_a|^2dk = \int4\sin^2ak\,dk = \infty$: the integrand does not decay at all, so
$\Delta k = \infty$ and the inequality holds trivially. The theorem's hypothesis $f' \in L^2$ fails, the
derivative of the box being a pair of deltas (@sec-distributions); a jump in $f$ means $\hat f \sim 1/k$, and
$k^2/k^2$ is not integrable. Smoothing the box by convolution with a narrow Gaussian makes $\Delta k$ finite but
large.
:::
