:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The proof of the inequality is short but each step uses something from this chapter, and writing it out in full
is the best way to own it. The first exercise asks for the details, including the uncentred case and the case
of equality.

::: {#exr-ft-uncertainty-proof}
#### The proof in detail

Justify each step of the proof of @thm-uncertainty, extend it to the uncentred case with means $\bar x$ and $\bar
k$, and solve the equality condition $f' = -cxf$ to show that the extremal functions are the Gaussians
$Ce^{i\bar kx}e^{-(x - \bar x)^2/2\sigma^2}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Plancherel applied to $f'$, whose transform is $ik\hat f$, gives $\int k^2|\hat f|^2 = 2\pi\int|f'|^2$; the
integration by parts needs $x|f|^2 \to 0$ at infinity, which holds since $xf$ and $f$ are square integrable and
$f$ is $C^1$ (so $x|f|^2$ is integrable with integrable derivative); Cauchy-Schwarz is $|\int x\bar ff'| \leq
(\int x^2|f|^2)^{1/2}(\int|f'|^2)^{1/2}$ (@def-bilinear-form). For the uncentred case apply the centred result to
$e^{-i\bar kx}f(x + \bar x)$, whose transform is $\hat f(k + \bar k)e^{i(k + \bar k)\bar x}$, with the same
widths about the shifted means. Equality in Cauchy-Schwarz means $f' = \lambda xf$ with $\lambda$ a constant, and
equality in $-2\operatorname{Re}\int x\bar ff' \leq 2|\int x\bar ff'|$ means $\lambda < 0$ real, so $f =
Ce^{-|\lambda|x^2/2}$; undoing the shift and modulation gives the stated family.
:::

$\tfrac52$, the values $n + \tfrac12$ of the harmonic-oscillator energies in units where $\hbar = \omega = 1$:

The product of widths does not change under scaling, translation or modulation, which is why the inequality has
a universal constant. The third exercise proves this invariance and uses it to reduce every Gaussian to the
standard one.

::: {#exr-ft-uncertainty-scaling}
#### Invariance of the product

Show that $\Delta x\,\Delta k$ is unchanged when $f(x)$ is replaced by $f(\lambda x)$, by $f(x - a)$ (with the
centred definitions about the new mean) or by $e^{ibx}f(x)$, and deduce from the single case $e^{-x^2/2}$ that
every Gaussian has product $\tfrac12$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Under $f(\lambda x)$, the substitution $u = \lambda x$ gives $(\Delta x)^2 \mapsto (\Delta x)^2/\lambda^2$, while
the transform becomes $\hat f(k/\lambda)/|\lambda|$ and $(\Delta k)^2 \mapsto \lambda^2(\Delta k)^2$; the product
is unchanged. A translation shifts $\bar x$ by $a$ and leaves $|\hat f|$ unchanged (the phase $e^{-ika}$ has
modulus $1$), so both centred widths are unchanged; a modulation shifts $\bar k$ by $b$ and leaves $|f|$
unchanged. Every Gaussian $Ce^{i\bar kx}e^{-(x - \bar x)^2/2\sigma^2}$ is obtained from $e^{-x^2/2}$ by scaling,
translating and modulating, so its product equals that of $e^{-x^2/2}$, which is $\tfrac12$ by
@exm-ft-uncertainty-gaussian with $\sigma = 1$.
:::

### The discrete Fourier transform

A computer stores a function by finitely many samples, and the integrals of the coefficients and of the transform become
finite sums. On $N$ equally spaced samples of a period the harmonics $e^{inx}$ become the $N$-th roots of unity, and
the orthogonality of @eq-mode-orthogonality becomes an exact identity between finite sums; the definition records the
resulting transform, which is exact and invertible in its own right [@izaac2018computational, Secs. 8.3.1-8.3.3].

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-fad-dft}
#### Discrete Fourier transform

The **discrete Fourier transform** of $(f_0, \dots, f_{N - 1}) \in \mathbb{C}^N$ is the sequence
$$
F_m = \sum_{n = 0}^{N - 1}f_n\,e^{-2\pi imn/N}, \qquad m \in \mathbb{Z},
$$ {#eq-fad-dft}
which is $N$-periodic, $F_{m + N} = F_m$, so that $F_0, \dots, F_{N - 1}$ determine it. The **discrete orthogonality**
$\sum_{m = 0}^{N - 1}e^{2\pi im(l - n)/N} = N\delta_{ln}$ for $0 \leq l, n < N$ gives the inversion $f_n =
\frac1N\sum_{m = 0}^{N - 1}F_me^{2\pi imn/N}$ and the **discrete Parseval identity** $\sum_n|f_n|^2 =
\frac1N\sum_m|F_m|^2$. For real $f_n$, $F_{N - m} = \overline{F_m}$, so $F_0$ and (for even $N$) $F_{N/2} =
\sum_n(-1)^nf_n$ are real and about half of the $F_m$ carry the information. If $f_n = f(2\pi n/N)$ are samples of a
trigonometric polynomial $f(x) = \sum_{|k| < N/2}c_ke^{ikx}$, then $F_m = Nc_m$ for $|m| < N/2$: the transform of the
samples computes the Fourier coefficients of @def-fourier-coefficient exactly, the index $m$ and $m - N$ standing for
the same wave number.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
For four samples the roots of unity are $\pm1$ and $\pm i$, and the transform is a $4 \times 4$ matrix that can be
written down at once. The first example applies it to the discrete analogues of the delta, the constant and a
translated delta.

::: {#exm-fad-four-points}
#### Four samples

For $N = 4$, $e^{-2\pi imn/4} = (-i)^{mn}$ and $F = Wf$ with $W = \begin{pmatrix}1 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -i & -1 & i \\ 1 &
-1 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & i & -1 & -i\end{pmatrix}$. The sample $(1, 0, 0, 0)$ has $F = (1, 1, 1, 1)$, the constant $(1, 1, 1,
1)$ has $F = (4, 0, 0, 0)$, the discrete forms of $\hat\delta = 1$ and $\hat1 = 2\pi\delta$ (@exm-dist-ft-delta,
@exm-dist-ft-constant), and the translate $(0, 1, 0, 0)$ has $F_m = (-i)^m$, the phase $e^{-2\pi im/4}$ of the translation
rule. One checks $W^\dagger W = 4\cdot1$, which is the discrete orthogonality.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

A trigonometric polynomial of low degree is recovered exactly from a few samples, and too few samples confuse its
harmonics. The second example samples $\cos^3x$ of @exm-fs-trig-polynomial with eight points and with four.

::: {#exm-fad-cos-cubed}
#### Eight samples of $\cos^3x$

$\cos^3x = \frac38(e^{ix} + e^{-ix}) + \frac18(e^{3ix} + e^{-3ix})$ has degree $3 < 8/2$, so the eight samples
$f_n = \cos^3(\pi n/4)$ have $F = 8(0, \frac38, 0, \frac18, 0, \frac18, 0, \frac38) = (0, 3, 0, 1, 0, 1, 0, 3)$, the
entries $m = 5, 7$ being the coefficients of $e^{-3ix}$ and $e^{-ix}$. With four samples, $e^{3ix}$ and $e^{-ix}$
take the same values at $x = \pi n/2$, since $3 \equiv -1 \pmod 4$, and the transform $F_1 = 4(\frac38 + \frac18) = 2$
adds the two coefficients: the samples cannot tell the harmonics apart. This confusion of wave numbers is the subject of
@prp-fad-sampling.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The sum @eq-fad-dft costs $N^2$ multiplications, and the structure of the roots of unity allows far fewer. The third
example derives the splitting of Cooley and Tukey, which Gauss had found in 1805 [@izaac2018computational, Sec. 8.5.1,
eqs. (8.45)-(8.49)].

::: {#exm-fad-cooley-tukey}
#### The fast Fourier transform

For even $N$, split @eq-fad-dft into even and odd $n$: $F_m = A_m + e^{-2\pi im/N}B_m$, where $A_m = \sum_lf_{2l}e^{-2\pi
iml/(N/2)}$ and $B_m = \sum_lf_{2l + 1}e^{-2\pi iml/(N/2)}$ are transforms of length $N/2$, hence $N/2$-periodic. Since
$e^{-2\pi i(m + N/2)/N} = -e^{-2\pi im/N}$, the **butterfly** $F_m = A_m + e^{-2\pi im/N}B_m$, $F_{m + N/2} = A_m -
e^{-2\pi im/N}B_m$ for $0 \leq m < N/2$ gives all $N$ values from two half-length transforms and $N/2$
multiplications. For $N = 2^b$ the splitting can be repeated $b$ times, and the count $M(N) = 2M(N/2) + N/2$ with
$M(1) = 0$ gives $M(N) = \frac N2\log_2N$: for $N = 1024$, $5120$ multiplications instead of about $10^6$. This is the
**fast Fourier transform**.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The inversion formula rests on a single finite geometric sum. The first exercise proves the discrete orthogonality and
derives inversion and Parseval from it.

::: {#exr-fad-orthogonality}
#### Discrete orthogonality

Show that $\frac1N\sum_{m = 0}^{N - 1}e^{2\pi im(l - n)/N} = \delta_{ln}$ for $0 \leq l, n < N$, by summing a
geometric series when $l \neq n$. Deduce the inversion formula and the discrete Parseval identity of @def-fad-dft, and
show that $W/\sqrt N$ is unitary, where $W_{mn} = e^{-2\pi imn/N}$ [@izaac2018computational, Problem P8.2].
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
For $l = n$ every term is $1$. For $l \neq n$, $r = e^{2\pi i(l - n)/N} \neq 1$ because $0 < |l - n| < N$, and $\sum_{m
= 0}^{N - 1}r^m = (r^N - 1)/(r - 1) = 0$ because $r^N = e^{2\pi i(l - n)} = 1$. Then $\frac1N\sum_mF_me^{2\pi imn/N} =
\sum_lf_l\frac1N\sum_me^{2\pi im(n - l)/N} = f_n$. The orthogonality says $W^\dagger W = N\cdot1$, so $U = W/\sqrt N$ is
unitary, and $\sum_m|F_m|^2 = \|Wf\|^2 = N\|f\|^2$ is Parseval; the inversion is $f = W^\dagger F/N$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The recursion of @exm-fad-cooley-tukey is short to program, and $e^{\cos x}$ of @exm-fs-coefficients-smooth has
known coefficients against which to test it. The second exercise implements the recursion in Sage and counts the
multiplications.

::: {#exr-fad-fft}
#### The fast transform in Sage

With Sage, implement the recursion of @exm-fad-cooley-tukey, check it against the direct sum @eq-fad-dft for the
samples of $e^{\cos x}$ with $N = 8$ and $N = 64$, count the multiplications for $N = 8, 64, 512$, and compare $F_m/N$ for
$N = 8$ with the Fourier coefficients $c_m = I_m(1)$. Which coefficient is worst, and why? [@izaac2018computational,
Sec. 8.5.1 and Problem P8.5]
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The recursion agrees with the direct sum to rounding and uses $\frac N2\log_2N$ multiplications, $2304$ against
$262144$ for $N = 512$:

{{< sage exr-fad-fft >}}

$F_m/N$ agrees with $I_m(1)$ to $2\times10^{-6}$ for $m \leq 3$, and the difference $F_1/8 - I_1(1)$ equals $I_7(1) +
I_9(1)$, the coefficients of the harmonics $e^{-7ix}$ and $e^{9ix}$ that coincide with $e^{ix}$ on the eight sample
points. The worst is $F_4/8 = 2I_4(1)$: the harmonics $e^{4ix}$ and $e^{-4ix}$ agree at the samples, and their
coefficients add.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The convolution theorem of @def-convolution has an exact discrete counterpart for periodic sequences, and it explains
why the transform diagonalises every translation-invariant linear map. The last exercise proves it and applies it to the
second difference.

::: {#exr-fad-circular}
#### Circular convolution

For $N$-periodic sequences define $(f \circledast g)_n = \sum_{l = 0}^{N - 1}f_lg_{n - l}$. Show that its transform is
$F_mG_m$. Deduce that every **circulant** matrix $C_{nl} = c_{n - l}$ has the eigenvectors $(e^{2\pi imn/N})_n$, and
find the eigenvalues of the periodic second difference $(\Delta f)_n = (f_{n + 1} - 2f_n + f_{n - 1})/h^2$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\sum_n\sum_lf_lg_{n - l}e^{-2\pi imn/N} = \sum_lf_le^{-2\pi iml/N}\sum_ng_{n - l}e^{-2\pi im(n - l)/N} = F_mG_m$, the
inner sum running over a full period of $g$ whatever $l$ is. A circulant matrix acts as $Cf = c \circledast f$, so on the
vector $e_m = (e^{2\pi imn/N})_n$, whose transform is $N\delta$ at $m$, it acts by multiplication with $\sum_lc_le^{-2\pi
iml/N}$. For the second difference $c_1 = c_{-1} = 1/h^2$, $c_0 = -2/h^2$, so the eigenvalues are $(2\cos(2\pi m/N) -
2)/h^2 = -\frac{4}{h^2}\sin^2\frac{\pi m}{N}$, which tends to $-(2\pi m/Nh)^2$, the eigenvalue $-k^2$ of $d^2/dx^2$, for
$m \ll N$. With walls instead of periodicity the same computation gives the grid levels of a particle in a box,
@prp-qmn-grid-box in the chapter on quantum mechanics.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

### Sampling and aliasing

The transform of samples is exact as a map of finite sequences, but as an approximation to Fourier coefficients or to
the transform it has an error, and @exm-fad-cos-cubed showed its mechanism: wave numbers that differ by a multiple of
the sampling rate are confused. The proposition makes this precise on the circle and on the line, using the Poisson
summation formula of @exr-ft-poisson-summation, and deduces the sampling theorem [@izaac2018computational, Secs.
8.1-8.1.2, 8.4].

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-fad-sampling}
#### Sampling and aliasing

(a) If $f$ is $2\pi$-periodic with $\sum_k|c_k| < \infty$ and $f_n = f(2\pi n/N)$, then $F_m/N = \sum_{j \in
\mathbb{Z}}c_{m + jN}$: each coefficient is contaminated by the coefficients of all wave numbers congruent to $m$ modulo $N$.
(b) If $f$ is a Schwartz function and $\Delta x > 0$, the **sampled transform** satisfies
$$
\Delta x\sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}}f(n\Delta x)\,e^{-ikn\Delta x} = \sum_{j \in \mathbb{Z}}\hat f\Big(k + \frac{2\pi
j}{\Delta x}\Big), \qquad k \in \mathbb{R} ,
$$ {#eq-fad-aliasing}
the **aliasing formula**: the Riemann sum for $\hat f(k)$ adds the copies of $\hat f$ shifted by multiples of
$2\pi/\Delta x$.
(c) (**Sampling theorem**) If moreover $\hat f$ is smooth and vanishes for $|k| \geq \pi/\Delta x$, the **Nyquist
wave number**, then the samples determine $f$:
$$
f(x) = \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}}f(n\Delta x)\,\frac{\sin(\pi(x - n\Delta x)/\Delta x)}{\pi(x - n\Delta x)/\Delta x} .
$$
*Proof.* (a) Insert $f_n = \sum_kc_ke^{2\pi ikn/N}$ into @eq-fad-dft and use the discrete orthogonality, which
selects $k \equiv m$; the absolute convergence allows the exchange of the sums. (b) Apply Poisson summation to $g(y) =
f(y\Delta x/2\pi)e^{-iky\Delta x/2\pi}$, whose transform is $\hat g(n) = \frac{2\pi}{\Delta x}\hat f(k + 2\pi n/\Delta
x)$. (c) A smooth compactly supported $\hat f$ makes $f$ a Schwartz function, and for $|k| < \pi/\Delta x$ only $j = 0$
contributes to @eq-fad-aliasing; the inversion formula over $|k| < \pi/\Delta x$ and $\int_{-\pi/\Delta x}^{\pi/\Delta
x}e^{ik(x - n\Delta x)}dk = 2\sin(\pi(x - n\Delta x)/\Delta x)/(x - n\Delta x)$ give the series.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
A wave sampled too sparsely masquerades as a slower one, which is the origin of the name. The first example finds the
alias of a given wave number and the condition under which none occurs.

::: {#exm-fad-alias-waves}
#### Which wave is seen

On the eight points $x_n = \pi n/4$, $\cos7x_n = \cos(8x_n - x_n) = \cos x_n$ and $\cos5x_n = \cos3x_n$, since $8x_n =
2\pi n$: by (a), a wave number $k$ is seen as the representative of $k$ modulo $N$ in $-N/2 < m \leq N/2$, and only
$|k| < N/2$ is seen correctly. In terms of the spacing $\Delta x = 2\pi/N$ the condition is $|k| < \pi/\Delta x$, the
Nyquist condition of (c): at least two samples per wavelength. A wheel filmed at $24$ frames per second that turns
$23$ times per second seems to turn backwards once per second for the same reason.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

For the Gaussian the shifted copies in @eq-fad-aliasing are themselves Gaussians and can be summed. The second example
shows that the Riemann sum for its integral is correct to many more digits than the size of the step suggests.

::: {#exm-fad-gaussian-sum}
#### The Riemann sum of a Gaussian

For $f = e^{-x^2/2\sigma^2}$, $\hat f(k) = \sigma\sqrt{2\pi}e^{-\sigma^2k^2/2}$ (@eq-gaussian-transform), and
@eq-fad-aliasing at $k = 0$ gives $\Delta x\sum_ne^{-n^2\Delta x^2/2\sigma^2} = \sigma\sqrt{2\pi}\bigl(1 +
2\sum_{j \geq 1}e^{-2\pi^2\sigma^2j^2/\Delta x^2}\bigr)$. For $\sigma = 1$ and the coarse step $\Delta x = 1$ the error
is $2\sqrt{2\pi}e^{-2\pi^2} = 1.3\times10^{-8}$ of the exact $\sqrt{2\pi}$: the error of the trapezoidal rule for a
smooth rapidly decaying function is governed by $\hat f$ at $2\pi/\Delta x$, not by a power of $\Delta x$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The transform of samples on an interval treats them as one period of a periodic function, and if the function does not
fit the interval, its periodic extension jumps. The third example shows the resulting spreading of a pure frequency and
how a window reduces it [@izaac2018computational, Sec. 8.4.2, eq. (8.43) and Figs. 8.4-8.6].

::: {#exm-fad-leakage}
#### Leakage and windows

Sample $\cos5x$ on $[0, 7)$ with $\Delta x = 0.1$, $N = 70$. The transform is that of the $7$-periodic function equal to
$\cos5x$ on $[0, 7)$, which jumps at $x = 7$ because $35/2\pi$ is not an integer; its coefficients decay like $1/m$, as
for the square wave (@exm-fs-coefficients-square), and the transform shows a spread of non-zero values around the
wave numbers $\pm5$ instead of two peaks (**leakage**). On an interval of length $2\pi$ the samples are exactly
periodic and only $m = \pm5$ appear. Multiplying by the **Hann window** $\sin^2(\pi x/7)$, which vanishes with its
derivative at both ends, makes the periodic extension $C^1$, and the coefficients decay like $1/m^3$
(@exm-fs-coefficients-smooth), at the price of broadening each peak over three neighbouring wave numbers.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The periodic case (a) needs only the discrete orthogonality, and the sampling theorem needs only the aliasing formula and
the inversion theorem. The first exercise carries out both proofs in detail.

::: {#exr-fad-aliasing-proof}
#### The proofs of aliasing and sampling

Prove (a) of @prp-fad-sampling. Prove (c) from (b) and @thm-fourier-inversion, justifying the exchange of the sum and
the integral, and show that the functions $s_n(x) = \operatorname{sinc}(\pi(x - n\Delta x)/\Delta x)$ are orthogonal on
the line with $\int s_ns_{n'}dx = \Delta x\,\delta_{nn'}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
(a) $F_m = \sum_{n = 0}^{N - 1}\sum_kc_ke^{2\pi i(k - m)n/N} = \sum_kc_k\sum_ne^{2\pi i(k - m)n/N}$, the exchange being
allowed because the double sum converges absolutely, and the inner sum is $N$ if $k \equiv m \pmod N$ and $0$
otherwise (@exr-fad-orthogonality). (c) For $|k| < \pi/\Delta x$ the right side of @eq-fad-aliasing is $\hat f(k)$,
because $\hat f(k + 2\pi j/\Delta x) = 0$ for $j \neq 0$. Then $f(x) = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\pi/\Delta x}^{\pi/\Delta
x}\hat f(k)e^{ikx}dk = \frac{\Delta x}{2\pi}\sum_nf(n\Delta x)\int_{-\pi/\Delta x}^{\pi/\Delta x}e^{ik(x - n\Delta
x)}dk$; the exchange is allowed because $\sum_n|f(n\Delta x)| < \infty$ for a Schwartz function and the interval is
bounded. The integral is $2\sin(\pi(x - n\Delta x)/\Delta x)/(x - n\Delta x)$. The transform of $s_n$ is $\Delta x\,e^{-ikn\Delta
x}$ on $|k| < \pi/\Delta x$ and $0$ outside (@exm-ft-box, translated and rescaled), so by @thm-plancherel $\int s_ns_{n'}
dx = \frac{\Delta x^2}{2\pi}\int_{-\pi/\Delta x}^{\pi/\Delta x}e^{-ik(n - n')\Delta x}dk = \Delta x\,\delta_{nn'}$: the
sampling series is an orthogonal expansion.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The momentum wave function of a quantum state is a Fourier transform, and in practice it is computed from samples with
the fast transform. The second exercise does this for the first excited state of the oscillator and watches the aliasing
error appear as the step grows.

::: {#exr-fad-oscillator-transform}
#### The transform of an oscillator state

For $\psi_1(x) = (4/\pi)^{1/4}xe^{-x^2/2}$ show that $\hat\psi_1(k) = -i\sqrt{2\pi}(4/\pi)^{1/4}ke^{-k^2/2}$. With
Sage, approximate it on the centred grid $x_n = (n - a)\Delta x$, $a = (N - 1)/2$, by the left side of
@eq-fad-aliasing at $k_m = (m - a)\Delta k$, $\Delta k = 2\pi/N\Delta x$, once as a direct sum and once with the fast
transform and the phase factors $e^{2\pi ian/N}$, $e^{2\pi i(m - a)a/N}$; compare with the exact transform for $\Delta
x = 0.05, 0.2, 0.5, 1, 1.5$, and check @eq-fad-aliasing at $k = 1$, $\Delta x = 1.5$ [@izaac2018computational, Secs. 8.1
and 8.3.4, and Problem P8.1].
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
By the multiplication rule of @def-fourier-transform, $\widehat{xe^{-x^2/2}} = i\frac{d}{dk}\sqrt{2\pi}e^{-k^2/2} =
-i\sqrt{2\pi}ke^{-k^2/2}$. Writing $x_nk_m = 2\pi(n - a)(m - a)/N$ and expanding the product separates the phase factors
from a one-sided transform of length $N$, so the two routes agree to rounding:

{{< sage exr-fad-oscillator-transform >}}

For $\Delta x \leq 0.5$ the error is tiny (at $\Delta x = 0.05$ the grid ends at $|x| = 5$, and the truncated tail
dominates); at $\Delta x = 1$ and $1.5$ the Nyquist wave number $\pi/\Delta x$ is no longer large compared with the
width of $\hat\psi_1$, and the error at $k = 1$ is exactly the sum of the shifted copies in @eq-fad-aliasing. (In the
reference the prefactor of the discretised transform should be $\Delta x$, not $\Delta k$, in eqs. (8.9), (8.19) and
Example 8.2.)
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The derivative rule $\widehat{f'} = ik\hat f$ turns differentiation into multiplication, and on samples it gives a
derivative whose error falls faster than any power of the step. The last exercise compares it with central differences
[@izaac2018computational, Sec. 8.2, eqs. (8.20)-(8.25), and Problems P8.3-P8.4].

::: {#exr-fad-spectral-derivative}
#### Fourier differentiation

With Sage, compute the first and second derivatives of $\psi_1$ on $N$ points of the periodic interval $[-10, 10)$ by
multiplying the discrete transform by $ik_m$ and $-k_m^2$, with $k_m = 2\pi m/20$ for $|m| < N/2$, and by central
differences, for $N = 16, 32, 64, 128, 256$. Repeat for the Hermite function $\psi_6 = H_6(x)e^{-x^2/2}/(2^66!\sqrt\pi)^{1/2}$,
with $H_6$ the Hermite polynomial of degree $6$. How do the errors scale, and why does $\psi_6$ need more points?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The central differences have the error $O(\Delta x^2)$, falling by $4$ when $N$ doubles. The Fourier derivative is
exact for trigonometric polynomials of degree below $N/2$ (@def-fad-dft), so its error is the part of $\psi$ beyond the
Nyquist wave number plus the aliased copies, which for a Gaussian-type function falls like $e^{-ck^2}$ at $k = \pi
N/20$: it reaches rounding error at $N = 64$:

{{< sage exr-fad-spectral-derivative >}}

The Hermite functions are eigenfunctions of the transform (@exr-ft-hermite-eigen), so $\hat\psi_6$ extends as far
as $\psi_6$, to $|k| \approx \sqrt{2\cdot6 + 1} \approx 3.6$ and beyond, against $\sqrt3 \approx 1.7$ for $\psi_1$; a more oscillatory function needs a higher Nyquist
wave number, hence more points, before the spectral accuracy sets in.
:::

**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.

### Worked computations

The transforms, rules and inequalities of this section are collected in one proposition. Every item is an exact
integral over the line, valid under sign conditions on the parameters; the widths are exact rational multiples of
$\sigma$ and the products are exact numbers.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-fourier-transform-values}
#### Transforms of the Gaussian, the box and the exponential

$\widehat{e^{-x^2/2\sigma^2}} = \sigma\sqrt{2\pi}e^{-\sigma^2k^2/2}$ and the inverse integral returns the Gaussian;
$\hat\chi_a = 2\sin ak/k$ and $\widehat{e^{-a|x|}} = 2a/(a^2 + k^2)$; $\widehat{f'} = ik\hat f$ for the Gaussian;
$\chi_a * \chi_a$ is the triangle $(2a - |x|)_+$, with $\int_{x - a}^a dy = 2a - x$ on $[0, 2a]$, and its
transform is $(2\sin ak/k)^2$; Plancherel for the box, $\frac{1}{2\pi}\int4\sin^2ak/k^2\,dk = 2a = \int\chi_a^2$;
$\Delta x = \sigma/\sqrt2$, $\Delta k = 1/\sigma\sqrt2$ and $\Delta x\Delta k = \tfrac12$ for the Gaussian, and
$\Delta x\Delta k = 1/\sqrt2$ for $e^{-a|x|}$.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
Each transform of the proposition is an improper integral, and it converges only under conditions on the
parameters. The first example states these conditions for the exponential and the Gaussian and shows what goes
wrong without them.

::: {#exm-ft-sage-assume}
#### Assumptions for improper integrals

$\int_0^\infty e^{-ax}e^{-ikx}dx = \frac{1}{a + ik}$ converges exactly when $\operatorname{Re}(a + ik) > 0$, which
for real $k$ means $a > 0$; adding the integral over $(-\infty, 0)$, which is $\frac{1}{a - ik}$, gives
$\widehat{e^{-a|x|}} = \frac{2a}{a^2 + k^2}$. For $a \leq 0$ the function does not decay and the integral diverges,
although the right-hand side still makes sense: the formula is not the transform of anything there. For the
Gaussian the integral converges for every complex $k$ once $\sigma > 0$, and $\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}e^{-\sigma^2k^2/2}$
holds for complex $k$ as well, both sides being analytic in $k$.
:::

The convolution rule can be tested on two boxes, where both sides are elementary. The second example computes the
triangle from the convolution integral, transforms it piece by piece and recovers the square of the sinc.

::: {#exm-ft-sage-convolution}
#### The convolution rule for two boxes

For $0 \leq x \leq 2a$ the boxes $[-a, a]$ and $[x - a, x + a]$ overlap in $[x - a, a]$, so $(\chi_a * \chi_a)(x) =
\int_{x - a}^a dy = 2a - x$, and by evenness the convolution is the triangle $(2a - |x|)_+$. Its transform is
$\int_{-2a}^0(2a + x)e^{-ikx}dx + \int_0^{2a}(2a - x)e^{-ikx}dx = 2\int_0^{2a}(2a - x)\cos kx\,dx = \frac{2 -
2\cos 2ak}{k^2}$, and $2 - 2\cos 2ak = 4\sin^2ak$ turns this into $(2\sin ak/k)^2 = \hat\chi_a^2$, as
@eq-convolution-theorem requires.
:::

The widths are ratios of second moments to integrals, and each moment is a Gaussian-type or a Lorentzian-type
integral with a closed form. The third example lists the four integrals behind the two uncertainty products.

::: {#exm-ft-sage-widths}
#### The widths as moment integrals

For the Gaussian, $\int x^2e^{-x^2/\sigma^2} = \sigma^3\sqrt\pi/2$ over $\int e^{-x^2/\sigma^2} = \sigma\sqrt\pi$
gives $\sigma^2/2$, and $\int k^2\cdot2\pi\sigma^2e^{-\sigma^2k^2}$ over $\int2\pi\sigma^2e^{-\sigma^2k^2}$ gives
$1/2\sigma^2$; for the exponential, $\int x^2e^{-2a|x|} = 1/2a^3$ over $1/a$ and $\int4a^2k^2/(a^2 + k^2)^2 =
2\pi a$ over $2\pi/a$. The squared products are $\tfrac{\sigma^2}{2}\cdot\tfrac{1}{2\sigma^2} = \tfrac14$ and
$\tfrac{1}{2a^2}\cdot a^2 = \tfrac12$, so $\Delta x\Delta k = \tfrac12$ and $1/\sqrt2$.
:::

The damped cosine is the function whose transform is the sum of two Lorentzians, the line shape of a damped
oscillator. The first exercise computes its transform in Sage and locates the two peaks.

::: {#exr-ft-damped-cosine}
#### The damped cosine

Compute the transform of $e^{-a|x|}\cos bx$ with Sage, show that it is the sum of two Lorentzians centred at $k =
\pm b$, and find the width at half maximum of each peak for $a \ll b$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
By the modulation rule, $\frac{a}{a^2 + (k - b)^2} + \frac{a}{a^2 + (k + b)^2}$; each Lorentzian $a/(a^2 + (k \mp
b)^2)$ has maximum $1/a$ and drops to half of it at $|k \mp b| = a$, so the full width at half maximum is $2a$,
the decay rate:

{{< sage exr-ft-damped-cosine >}}
:::

The hyperbolic secant is, like the Gaussian, its own transform up to scaling, and it is the shape of the soliton
of several wave equations. The second exercise asks for its transform, which is a residue computation over the
poles of $\operatorname{sech}$, with Sage as a numerical check.

::: {#exr-ft-sech}
#### The hyperbolic secant

Show that $\widehat{\operatorname{sech} x} = \pi\operatorname{sech}(\pi k/2)$ by summing the residues of
$\operatorname{sech} z\,e^{-ikz}$ at $z = i\pi(n + \tfrac12)$, $n \geq 0$, and check the formula numerically in Sage
at a few values of $k$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
For $k < 0$ close the contour in the upper half-plane; $\operatorname{sech} z = 1/\cosh z$ has simple poles at
$z_n = i\pi(n + \tfrac12)$ with residues $1/\sinh z_n = 1/(i\sin\pi(n + \tfrac12)) = (-1)^n/i$, so
$\int\operatorname{sech} x\,e^{-ikx}dx = 2\pi i\sum_{n \geq 0}\frac{(-1)^n}{i}e^{\pi k(n + 1/2)} =
2\pi\frac{e^{\pi k/2}}{1 + e^{\pi k}} = \frac{\pi}{\cosh(\pi k/2)}$, a geometric series since $e^{\pi k} < 1$;
the case $k > 0$ follows by evenness. Sage's symbolic integrator does not return this closed form, and the
check is numerical:

{{< sage exr-ft-sech >}}
:::

In several variables the transform is taken in each coordinate, and a radial function has a radial transform.
The third exercise works out the three-dimensional transform of a radial function as a one-dimensional sine
transform and applies it to the Yukawa function of @prp-greens-laplacian.

::: {#exr-ft-radial}
#### Radial functions in three dimensions

Define $\hat f(\mathbf k) = \int_{\mathbb{R}^3}f(\mathbf x)e^{-i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x}d^3x$. Show that for a
radial $f(r)$ the transform is radial with $\hat f(k) = \frac{4\pi}{k}\int_0^\infty f(r)\sin(kr)\,r\,dr$, and
use it to show that the transform of $e^{-mr}/(4\pi r)$ is $1/(k^2 + m^2)$ and that of the Gaussian
$e^{-r^2/2\sigma^2}$ is $(\sigma\sqrt{2\pi})^3e^{-\sigma^2k^2/2}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
In spherical coordinates with the polar axis along $\mathbf k$ (@thm-change-of-variables), $\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x
= kr\cos\theta$ and $\hat f = \int_0^\infty f(r)r^2dr\int_0^{2\pi}d\varphi\int_0^\pi e^{-ikr\cos\theta}\sin\theta\,d\theta
= 2\pi\int_0^\infty f(r)r^2\frac{2\sin kr}{kr}dr$. For the Yukawa function, $\frac{4\pi}{k}\int_0^\infty\frac{e^{-mr}}{4\pi
r}\sin(kr)\,r\,dr = \frac1k\operatorname{Im}\int_0^\infty e^{-(m - ik)r}dr = \frac1k\operatorname{Im}\frac{1}{m -
ik} = \frac{1}{k^2 + m^2}$, the momentum-space Green's function of @prp-greens-laplacian. For the Gaussian the
three Cartesian integrals factorise and each gives $\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}e^{-\sigma^2k_i^2/2}$ by
@eq-gaussian-transform.
:::

## Distributions {#sec-distributions}

The delta function of @def-dirac-delta, the transform of the constant function, and the derivative of a function
with a jump are not functions, but they are all linear functionals on smooth test functions, and that is the
definition that makes the formal computations of physics rigorous. This section defines test functions and
distributions, their derivatives and Fourier transforms, and the principal value, with the figure showing two
sequences of functions that converge to the delta; the identities obtained along the way are collected in the
proposition at the end.

![Two sequences converging to the delta function. Left: the Gaussians $g_\varepsilon(x) =
e^{-x^2/\varepsilon^2}/(\varepsilon\sqrt\pi)$ of unit integral, concentrating as $\varepsilon \to 0$. Right: the
Fourier kernels $\delta_L(x) = \sin(Lx)/(\pi x) = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-L}^Le^{ikx}dk$, also of unit integral,
oscillating more and more rapidly as $L \to \infty$ while their action on every test function tends to its value
at $0$. Generated by `figures/delta_sequence.sage`.](figures/delta_sequence.svg){#fig-delta-sequence width=95%}

{{< interactive delta_sequence 460 >}}

### Test functions

A distribution is defined by what it does to nice functions, so the first thing to fix is the class of nice
functions. The definition introduces the two standard classes, the smooth functions of compact support and the
rapidly decreasing functions of Schwartz, and what it means for a sequence of them to converge.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-test-function}
#### Test function

A **test function** is a smooth function $\varphi : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{C}$ that vanishes outside a bounded
interval (**compact support**); the space of test functions is written $\mathcal{D}$. A **Schwartz function** is
a smooth function such that $x^m\varphi^{(n)}(x)$ is bounded for all $m, n \geq 0$ (all derivatives decay faster
than any power); the space of Schwartz functions is $\mathcal{S} \supset \mathcal{D}$, and it is closed under
differentiation, multiplication by polynomials and the Fourier transform (@exr-dist-schwartz-transform). A
sequence $\varphi_j \to \varphi$ **in $\mathcal{S}$** if $\sup_x|x^m(\varphi_j - \varphi)^{(n)}| \to 0$ for every
$m, n$, and **in $\mathcal{D}$** if moreover all $\varphi_j$ vanish outside one fixed interval. The same
definitions apply on $\mathbb{R}^n$ with multi-indices.
:::

That non-zero test functions exist at all is not obvious, since a function vanishing on a half-line together
with all its derivatives has zero Taylor series there. The first example exhibits the standard bump, which is
smooth but not analytic.

::: {#exm-dist-bump}
#### The bump function

$\varphi(x) = e^{-1/(1 - x^2)}$ for $|x| < 1$ and $\varphi(x) = 0$ for $|x| \geq 1$ is a test function: it is
smooth, every derivative at $\pm1$ being $0$ from both sides (@exr-dist-bump), and it vanishes outside $[-1, 1]$.
It is not analytic at $\pm1$, where its Taylor series is identically zero (@sec-analytic-continuation); scaled
and translated bumps $\varphi((x - a)/\varepsilon)$ are supported in $[a - \varepsilon, a + \varepsilon]$.
:::

Schwartz functions need not vanish anywhere, and the Gaussian is the prototype; the example also lists functions
that fail the definition, to mark its boundary. The second example compares several candidates.

::: {#exm-dist-schwartz-gaussian}
#### Schwartz functions and non-examples

$e^{-x^2/2}$, $p(x)e^{-x^2/2}$ for every polynomial $p$, and the Hermite functions are Schwartz: $x^m$ times any
derivative is a polynomial times a Gaussian, which is bounded. $e^{-|x|}$ is not, since it is not differentiable
at $0$; $1/(1 + x^2)$ is smooth but decays only like $x^{-2}$, so $x^3/(1 + x^2)$ is unbounded; and $e^{-x^2}\sin
e^{x^2}$ decays but its derivative $-2xe^{-x^2}\sin e^{x^2} + 2x\cos e^{x^2}$ does not. Every test function is a
Schwartz function.
:::

The Fourier transform exchanges decay with smoothness, which is why the Schwartz space, with both, is the natural
home of the transform. The third example makes the exchange explicit through the rules of @def-fourier-transform.

::: {#exm-dist-schwartz-closed}
#### Decay against smoothness

By the derivative and multiplication rules, $\widehat{\varphi^{(n)}} = (ik)^n\hat\varphi$ and $\widehat{x^m\varphi}
= i^m\hat\varphi^{(m)}$: derivatives of $\varphi$ become powers of $k$ and powers of $x$ become derivatives in $k$.
So $k^n\hat\varphi^{(m)}(k) = (-i)^n i^m\,\widehat{(x^m\varphi)^{(n)}}$ is bounded by $\int|(x^m\varphi)^{(n)}|$,
finite for a Schwartz $\varphi$: the transform of a Schwartz function is Schwartz, and inversion shows the
transform is a bijection of $\mathcal{S}$ (@exr-dist-schwartz-transform). The transform of a test function is
Schwartz but never a test function, by the identity theorem for its entire extension.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The smoothness of the bump at the edge of its support is a statement about the derivatives of $e^{-1/t}$ as $t
\to 0^+$, each of which is a rational function times the exponential. The first exercise proves it and lets Sage
display the first few derivatives.

::: {#exr-dist-bump}
#### Smoothness of the bump

Show that every derivative of $h(t) = e^{-1/t}$ ($t > 0$), extended by $0$ for $t \leq 0$, has the form
$p_n(1/t)e^{-1/t}$ with $p_n$ a polynomial, deduce that $h$ is smooth on $\mathbb{R}$ with $h^{(n)}(0) = 0$, and
conclude for the bump $\varphi(x) = h(1 - x^2)$; display $h', h'', h'''$ with Sage and their limits at $0^+$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$h' = t^{-2}e^{-1/t}$, and if $h^{(n)} = p_n(1/t)e^{-1/t}$ then $h^{(n+1)} = [-t^{-2}p_n'(1/t) +
t^{-2}p_n(1/t)]e^{-1/t}$, of the same form with $p_{n+1}(u) = u^2(p_n(u) - p_n'(u))$. Since $u^me^{-u} \to 0$ as
$u \to \infty$, $h^{(n)}(t) \to 0$ as $t \to 0^+$ for every $n$; by induction and the mean value theorem the
one-sided derivatives at $0$ exist and vanish, so $h$ is smooth with all derivatives zero at $0$. The composite
$\varphi(x) = h(1 - x^2)$ is smooth by the chain rule, and vanishes with all derivatives at $|x| = 1$:

{{< sage exr-dist-bump >}}
:::

The claim that the transform maps $\mathcal{S}$ onto itself continuously underlies the definition of the Fourier
transform of a distribution. The second exercise asks for the estimate behind it and for continuity with respect
to convergence in $\mathcal{S}$.

::: {#exr-dist-schwartz-transform}
#### The transform on the Schwartz space

Prove that $\sup_k|k^n\hat\varphi^{(m)}(k)| \leq \int|(x^m\varphi)^{(n)}|\,dx \leq C\sum_{j \leq n, i \leq m +
2}\sup_x|x^i\varphi^{(j)}|$ for Schwartz $\varphi$, conclude that $\varphi \mapsto \hat\varphi$ maps $\mathcal{S}$
to $\mathcal{S}$ continuously, and that it is a bijection with inverse $\check\varphi$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The first inequality is @exm-dist-schwartz-closed together with $|\hat g(k)| \leq \int|g|$. For the second, $\int|g|
\leq \sup|(1 + x^2)g|\int\frac{dx}{1 + x^2} = \pi\sup|(1 + x^2)g|$ with $g = (x^m\varphi)^{(n)}$, and by the
Leibniz rule $(x^m\varphi)^{(n)}$ is a sum of terms $x^{m - l}\varphi^{(n - l)}$ with constant coefficients, so
$(1 + x^2)g$ is bounded by a sum of the seminorms $\sup|x^i\varphi^{(j)}|$ with $i \leq m + 2$, $j \leq n$. Hence
every seminorm of $\hat\varphi$ is bounded by finitely many seminorms of $\varphi$, which is continuity for the
convergence of @def-test-function; the inverse transform satisfies the same bounds, and @thm-fourier-inversion
shows that the two maps are mutually inverse on $\mathcal{S}$, where all hypotheses hold.
:::

Convolving with a scaled test function of unit integral smooths a function without changing it much, and this
mollification is how rough functions are approximated by smooth ones. The third exercise establishes the two
properties of a mollifier and the consequence that test functions are dense.

::: {#exr-dist-mollifier}
#### Mollifiers

Let $\varphi$ be a non-negative test function with $\int\varphi = 1$ and $\varphi_\varepsilon(x) =
\varphi(x/\varepsilon)/\varepsilon$. Show that $f * \varphi_\varepsilon$ is smooth for every locally integrable
$f$, that $f * \varphi_\varepsilon \to f$ uniformly on bounded intervals if $f$ is continuous, and that $f *
\varphi_\varepsilon$ is a test function if $f$ is continuous with compact support.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$(f * \varphi_\varepsilon)(x) = \int f(y)\varphi_\varepsilon(x - y)dy$ may be differentiated under the integral
sign any number of times (@thm-differentiation-under-integral), the $x$-derivatives falling on the smooth
$\varphi_\varepsilon$ and the integral extending only over the bounded set where $\varphi_\varepsilon(x - y) \neq
0$. Since $\int\varphi_\varepsilon = 1$ and $\varphi_\varepsilon$ is supported in $[-\varepsilon C, \varepsilon
C]$, $|(f * \varphi_\varepsilon)(x) - f(x)| \leq \int|f(x - y) - f(x)|\varphi_\varepsilon(y)dy \leq \sup_{|y| \leq
\varepsilon C}|f(x - y) - f(x)|$, which tends to $0$ uniformly on bounded intervals by uniform continuity of $f$
there. If $f$ vanishes outside $[-R, R]$ then $f * \varphi_\varepsilon$ vanishes outside $[-R - \varepsilon C, R +
\varepsilon C]$ and is smooth, hence a test function; this is the sequence of @exr-ft-inversion-gaussian with a
compactly supported kernel in place of the Gaussian.
:::

### Distributions

A distribution is a continuous linear functional on test functions, and every locally integrable function is one
by integration; the delta is the simplest one that is not. The definition fixes the vocabulary, the notion of
convergence of distributions, and the fact that the delta is a limit of functions.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-distribution}
#### Distribution

A **distribution** is a linear map $T : \mathcal{D} \to \mathbb{C}$, written $T(\varphi)$ or $\langle T,
\varphi\rangle$, that is continuous: $T(\varphi_j) \to T(\varphi)$ whenever $\varphi_j \to \varphi$ in
$\mathcal{D}$. A **tempered distribution** is a continuous linear map $\mathcal{S} \to \mathbb{C}$; it restricts to
a distribution, and tempered distributions are the ones with Fourier transforms. Every locally integrable $f$ of
at most polynomial growth defines the **regular** tempered distribution $T_f(\varphi) = \int f\varphi\,dx$, and
$f$ is identified with $T_f$; the **Dirac delta** is $\delta(\varphi) = \varphi(0)$, and $\delta_a(\varphi) =
\varphi(a)$ is written $\delta(x - a)$ (@def-dirac-delta). Distributions $T_j$ **converge** to $T$ if $T_j(\varphi)
\to T(\varphi)$ for every test function; the point of the definition is that a sequence of functions can converge
as distributions to something that is not a function, as $g_\varepsilon \to \delta$ in @fig-delta-sequence.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
Which functions define tempered distributions is a matter of growth at infinity, since the test functions decay
fast but not infinitely fast. The first example sorts the common functions into the tempered and the
non-tempered.

::: {#exm-dist-regular}
#### Regular distributions

Polynomials, $|x|^s$ for $s > -1$, $\log|x|$, bounded functions and periodic piecewise continuous functions are all
tempered, since $\int|f\varphi| \leq \sup|(1 + x^2)^N\varphi|\int|f|(1 + x^2)^{-N}$ is finite for $N$ large; the
step function $\theta$ and the sign function are tempered. $e^{x^2}$ and $e^{|x|}$ define distributions on
$\mathcal{D}$ but not tempered ones, since $\int e^{x^2}\varphi$ diverges for $\varphi = e^{-x^2/2}$ and
$\int e^{|x|}\varphi$ diverges for $\varphi = e^{-\sqrt{1 + x^2}}$, both Schwartz functions; and $1/x$ is not
locally integrable at $0$, so it defines no regular distribution at all, a gap that @def-principal-value fills.
:::

The delta is a limit in many ways, and each approximating sequence is a kernel that appears somewhere in analysis.
The second example lists the Gaussian, the Fourier kernel of the figure, the Lorentzian and the Dirichlet kernel,
with the common mechanism.

::: {#exm-dist-delta-limits}
#### Sequences converging to $\delta$

$g_\varepsilon = e^{-x^2/\varepsilon^2}/(\varepsilon\sqrt\pi)$, the Lorentzians $\frac{\varepsilon}{\pi(x^2 +
\varepsilon^2)}$ and the heat kernel $K_t$ all have unit integral and concentrate at $0$, so $\int g_\varepsilon\varphi
\to \varphi(0)$ by the argument of @exr-ft-inversion-gaussian; for $\varphi = \cos x$ the Gaussian integral is
$e^{-\varepsilon^2/4} \to 1$ (@prp-distribution-identities). The Fourier kernel $\delta_L = \sin(Lx)/(\pi x)$ also
has unit integral but is not positive; it still converges to $\delta$, by the Riemann-Lebesgue lemma applied to
$(\varphi(x) - \varphi(0))/x$, and exactly so on $\cos x$ for every $L > 1$. On the circle, $D_N/2\pi \to \delta$
in the same sense, which is Dirichlet's theorem.
:::

Composing the delta with a function is defined by substitution in the integral, and the rules of
@exr-delta-scaling become theorems about regular sequences. The third example records them in the present
language and adds the two-dimensional delta in polar coordinates.

::: {#exm-dist-delta-composition}
#### Composition rules

$\delta(ax) = \delta(x)/|a|$ because $\int g_\varepsilon(ax)\varphi(x)dx = \frac{1}{|a|}\int
g_\varepsilon(y)\varphi(y/a)dy \to \varphi(0)/|a|$; more generally $\delta(h(x)) = \sum_i\delta(x -
x_i)/|h'(x_i)|$ over the simple zeros of $h$, so $\delta(x^2 - a^2) = [\delta(x - a) + \delta(x + a)]/2|a|$. In
the plane, $\delta^2(\mathbf x) = \delta(x)\delta(y)$ becomes $\delta(r)/(2\pi r)$ in polar coordinates, since
$\int\delta^2\varphi\,d^2x = \varphi(0)$ must equal $\int_0^\infty\int_0^{2\pi}\frac{\delta(r)}{2\pi r}\varphi\,
r\,d\theta\,dr$ with the convention $\int_0^\infty\delta(r)dr = 1$.
:::

Different test functions probe the limiting distribution differently, and computing the Gaussian integrals for
several of them, exactly in $\varepsilon$, shows how the limit is approached. The first exercise does this for
polynomial, trigonometric and exponential test functions, and for the Fourier kernel.

::: {#exr-dist-delta-limits}
#### The delta sequences against test functions

Compute $\int g_\varepsilon\varphi$ exactly for $\varphi = x^2 + 1$, $\varphi = e^{x}$ and $\varphi = \cos 2x$ with
Sage, take the limits $\varepsilon \to 0$, and compute $\int\delta_L(x)\cos 2x\,dx$ as a function of $L$ to see
where it becomes exactly $1$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The three integrals are $1 + \varepsilon^2/2$, $e^{\varepsilon^2/4}$ and $e^{-\varepsilon^2}$, each tending to
$\varphi(0) = 1$; the Fourier kernel gives $\int\delta_L\cos 2x\,dx = \tfrac12[\operatorname{sgn}(L + 2) +
\operatorname{sgn}(L - 2)]$, which is $0$ for $L < 2$, $\tfrac12$ at $L = 2$ and exactly $1$ for $L > 2$, the
transform of the kernel being a box of half-width $L$ (@exm-ft-duality):

{{< sage exr-dist-delta-limits >}}
:::

The delta is genuinely not a function, and the proof is a short argument with a narrow bump. The second exercise
asks for it, and for the related fact that a distribution supported at a point is determined by finitely many
derivatives at that point.

::: {#exr-dist-not-function}
#### The delta is not a function

Prove that there is no locally integrable $f$ with $\int f\varphi = \varphi(0)$ for all test functions $\varphi$,
and show that if a distribution $T$ satisfies $T(\varphi) = 0$ whenever $\varphi$ vanishes near $0$ and $T(\varphi)$
depends only on $\varphi(0)$, then $T = c\,\delta$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Take $\varphi_\varepsilon(x) = \varphi(x/\varepsilon)$ with $\varphi$ the bump of @exm-dist-bump; then
$\int f\varphi_\varepsilon \to 0$ as $\varepsilon \to 0$, since $|\int f\varphi_\varepsilon| \leq
\varphi(0)\int_{-\varepsilon}^\varepsilon|f|$ and the integral of a locally integrable function over a shrinking
interval tends to $0$; but $\varphi_\varepsilon(0) = \varphi(0) = e^{-1} \neq 0$ for every $\varepsilon$, a
contradiction. For the second statement, $\varphi \mapsto T(\varphi)$ is a linear function of the number
$\varphi(0)$, hence of the form $c\varphi(0)$ with $c = T(\psi)$ for any $\psi$ with $\psi(0) = 1$. (Without the
second hypothesis a distribution supported at $0$ is a finite combination $\sum_{n \leq N}c_n\delta^{(n)}$, a
theorem not proved here.)
:::

A periodic array of deltas is a tempered distribution, and its Fourier series is the formal series of
@exr-fs-termwise-differentiation with all coefficients equal. The third exercise proves this identity, which is
Poisson summation in distributional form.

::: {#exr-dist-comb}
#### The Dirac comb

Show that $\text{Ш}(x) = \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}}\delta(x - 2\pi n)$ is a tempered distribution and that
$\text{Ш} = \frac{1}{2\pi}\sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}}e^{inx}$ as distributions, that is, $\sum_n\varphi(2\pi n) =
\frac{1}{2\pi}\sum_n\hat\varphi(-n)$ for every Schwartz $\varphi$; deduce that the derivative of the sawtooth is
$1 - 2\pi\,\text{Ш}(x - \pi)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$|\sum_n\varphi(2\pi n)| \leq \sup|(1 + x^2)\varphi|\sum_n(1 + 4\pi^2n^2)^{-1}$ is bounded by a seminorm, so the
comb is tempered. The pairing of $\frac{1}{2\pi}\sum_ne^{inx}$ with $\varphi$ is, term by term,
$\frac{1}{2\pi}\sum_n\int\varphi e^{inx} = \frac{1}{2\pi}\sum_n\hat\varphi(-n)$, and Poisson summation
(@exr-ft-poisson-summation) says this equals $\sum_n\varphi(2\pi n)$, the pairing with the comb; the series
converges as distributions because its partial sums are the Dirichlet kernels, whose pairings converge. The
sawtooth $f(x) = x$ on $(-\pi, \pi)$ has $f' = 1$ away from the jumps and a jump of $-2\pi$ at each odd multiple
of $\pi$; by @exm-dist-step-derivative each jump contributes $-2\pi\delta$ there, giving $1 - 2\pi\sum_n\delta(x -
(2n + 1)\pi)$, whose Fourier series $1 - \sum_n(-1)^ne^{inx} = 2\sum_{n \geq 1}(-1)^{n+1}\cos nx$ is the
divergent series found by differentiating term by term.
:::

### Derivatives of distributions

Every distribution has derivatives of all orders, defined by moving the derivative onto the test function with a
sign, as integration by parts suggests. The definition records this, the product with a smooth function, and the
Leibniz rule, with the identity $x\delta' = -\delta$ as the first non-obvious consequence.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-distributional-derivative}
#### Distributional derivative

The **derivative** of a distribution $T$ is the distribution $T'(\varphi) = -T(\varphi')$, so that $T^{(n)}(\varphi)
= (-1)^nT(\varphi^{(n)})$; for a $C^1$ function $f$ this agrees with the classical derivative, since $\int
f\varphi'\,dx = -\int f'\varphi\,dx$ with no boundary terms. The **product** of $T$ with a smooth function $\psi$
of polynomial growth (with all derivatives) is $(\psi T)(\varphi) = T(\psi\varphi)$, and the **Leibniz rule**
$(\psi T)' = \psi'T + \psi T'$ holds. Differentiation is continuous: $T_j \to T$ implies $T_j' \to T'$, so a
convergent sequence of functions may be differentiated term by term as distributions, whatever happens to the
classical derivatives.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The derivative of the step function is the delta, the identity that makes Green's functions work
(@sec-greens-functions). The first example computes it from the definition and extends it to any function with
a jump.

::: {#exm-dist-step-derivative}
#### $\theta' = \delta$

$\theta'(\varphi) = -\int_0^\infty\varphi'(x)dx = \varphi(0) = \delta(\varphi)$, since $\varphi$ vanishes at
infinity (@prp-distribution-identities, with $\varphi = (1 + x)e^{-x^2}$). If $f$ is $C^1$ away from $a$ with a
jump $J = f(a^+) - f(a^-)$, the same computation gives $f' = \{f'\} + J\delta(x - a)$, where $\{f'\}$ is the
classical derivative away from $a$: for the square wave, $f' = 2\sum_n(-1)^n\delta(x - n\pi)$.
:::

Differentiating twice turns a kink into a delta, which is the one-dimensional model of a point source. The second
example takes $|x|$ and then the Green's function of $-d^2/dx^2$.

::: {#exm-dist-abs-derivative}
#### $|x|'' = 2\delta$

$|x|' = \operatorname{sgn} x = 2\theta - 1$ (no jump, so no delta), and $|x|'' = 2\theta' = 2\delta$: the kink of
$|x|$ at $0$ has slope jump $2$. Hence $u = -\tfrac12|x - \xi|$ solves $-u'' = \delta(x - \xi)$, a fundamental
solution of $-d^2/dx^2$ (@def-fundamental-solution), and adding the linear function that fixes the boundary values
gives the Dirichlet Green's function of @prp-greens-laplacian, whose slope jump $-1$ at $\xi$ is this delta.
:::

The derivative of the delta is a dipole: it measures the slope of the test function, with a sign. The third
example computes its action, verifies $x\delta' = -\delta$, and shows how $\delta'$ arises as a limit of the
derivatives of Gaussians.

::: {#exm-dist-delta-derivative}
#### The derivative of the delta

$\delta'(\varphi) = -\varphi'(0)$ and $\delta^{(n)}(\varphi) = (-1)^n\varphi^{(n)}(0)$. By the Leibniz rule
$(x\delta)' = \delta + x\delta'$ and $x\delta = 0$ (since $(x\delta)(\varphi) = 0\cdot\varphi(0)$), so $x\delta' = -
\delta$; directly, $(x\delta')(\varphi) = \delta'(x\varphi) = -(x\varphi)'(0) = -\varphi(0)$. As a limit,
$g_\varepsilon' \to \delta'$ by continuity of differentiation: $\int g_\varepsilon'\sin x\,dx = -e^{-\varepsilon^2/4}
\to -1 = -\cos 0$ and $\int xg_\varepsilon'\cos x\,dx \to -1$ (@prp-distribution-identities).
:::

The Leibniz rule and the identity $x\delta = 0$ are the two facts that let one compute with products of smooth
functions and deltas. The second exercise proves both, along with their consequences for $\delta'$ and
$\delta''$.

::: {#exr-dist-product-rule}
#### Products with smooth functions

Prove the Leibniz rule $(\psi T)' = \psi'T + \psi T'$ from the definitions, show $\psi\delta = \psi(0)\delta$,
$\psi\delta' = \psi(0)\delta' - \psi'(0)\delta$, and find $x^2\delta''$ and $x\delta''$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$(\psi T)'(\varphi) = -T(\psi\varphi') = -T((\psi\varphi)' - \psi'\varphi) = T'(\psi\varphi) + T(\psi'\varphi) =
(\psi T' + \psi'T)(\varphi)$. $(\psi\delta)(\varphi) = \psi(0)\varphi(0)$; $(\psi\delta')(\varphi) =
-(\psi\varphi)'(0) = -\psi'(0)\varphi(0) - \psi(0)\varphi'(0) = (\psi(0)\delta' - \psi'(0)\delta)(\varphi)$. With
$\psi = x^2$: $(x^2\delta'')(\varphi) = (x^2\varphi)''(0) = 2\varphi(0)$, so $x^2\delta'' = 2\delta$; with $\psi =
x$: $(x\varphi)''(0) = 2\varphi'(0)$, so $x\delta'' = -2\delta'$. In general $x^n\delta^{(n)} = (-1)^nn!\,\delta$.
:::

A linear differential equation with a delta source is solved in distributions by a function with a kink, and the
kink condition replaces the source. The third exercise solves $u'' - u = \delta$ and verifies the result in Sage
through the jump of the derivative.

::: {#exr-dist-greens-ode}
#### A Green's function as a distribution

Find the bounded solution of $u'' - u = \delta$ on $\mathbb{R}$ by solving the homogeneous equation on each side
of $0$, imposing continuity and the jump of $u'$ that the delta requires; verify with Sage that $u = -e^{-|x|}/2$
satisfies $\int u(\varphi'' - \varphi) = \varphi(0)$ for $\varphi = e^{-x^2}$, and connect with
@def-greens-function.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Bounded solutions of $u'' = u$ on each side are $Ae^{-x}$ ($x > 0$) and $Be^{x}$ ($x < 0$); continuity gives $A =
B$, and $u'' = \{u''\} + [u'](0)\delta$ with $[u'](0) = -A - A = -2A$ must produce $\delta$, so $A = -\tfrac12$ and
$u = -\tfrac12e^{-|x|}$. The distributional identity $u'' - u = \delta$ means $\int u(\varphi'' - \varphi) =
\varphi(0)$ for every test function, which Sage confirms for a Gaussian (the Gaussian is Schwartz rather than
compactly supported, which suffices since $u$ is tempered); the exact value contains an incomplete gamma function
that Sage does not reduce, and the comparison with $\varphi(0) = 1$ is made to twelve digits. The function $G(x, \xi) = -\tfrac12e^{-|x - \xi|}$ is
the Green's function of $d^2/dx^2 - 1$ on the line, the one-dimensional Yukawa potential with $m = 1$
(@prp-greens-laplacian):

{{< sage exr-dist-greens-ode >}}
:::

### The principal value

The function $1/x$ is not locally integrable, but the odd part of a test function around $0$ cancels its
singularity, and the resulting functional is the distribution that appears in every dispersion relation. The
definition introduces it, identifies it as the derivative of $\log|x|$, and records the Sokhotski-Plemelj formula
that splits $1/(x \mp i0)$ into a principal value and a delta.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-principal-value}
#### Principal value

The **principal value** of $1/x$ is the tempered distribution
$$
\operatorname{PV}\frac1x(\varphi) = \lim_{\varepsilon \to 0^+}\int_{|x| > \varepsilon}\frac{\varphi(x)}{x}dx =
\int_0^\infty\frac{\varphi(x) - \varphi(-x)}{x}dx,
$$ {#eq-principal-value}
the limit existing because the integrand of the last form is bounded near $0$ by $2\sup|\varphi'|$. It is the
distributional derivative of $\log|x|$, it satisfies $x\cdot\operatorname{PV}\frac1x = 1$, and the
**Sokhotski-Plemelj formula** states that, as distributions,
$$
\lim_{\varepsilon \to 0^+}\frac{1}{x \mp i\varepsilon} = \operatorname{PV}\frac1x \pm i\pi\delta(x),
$$ {#eq-sokhotski-plemelj}
since $\frac{1}{x \mp i\varepsilon} = \frac{x}{x^2 + \varepsilon^2} \pm i\frac{\varepsilon}{x^2 + \varepsilon^2}$,
the real part tending to the principal value and the imaginary part being $\pi$ times a delta sequence
(@exm-dist-delta-limits). The same definition gives $\operatorname{PV}\int_a^b\frac{\varphi(x)}{x - c}dx$ for $a <
c < b$ by removing a symmetric interval around $c$.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
A principal value of a definite integral through a simple pole is the symmetric limit, and for $1/x$ on an
interval it is a logarithm. The first example computes it and shows that the symmetric removal is what makes the
answer finite and unique.

::: {#exm-dist-pv-rational}
#### $\operatorname{PV}\int_{-1}^2 dx/x = \log 2$

$\int_{-1}^{-\varepsilon}\frac{dx}{x} + \int_\varepsilon^2\frac{dx}{x} = \log\varepsilon - \log1 + \log2 -
\log\varepsilon = \log2$ for every $\varepsilon$ (@prp-distribution-identities): the divergent logarithms cancel
because the removed interval is symmetric. Removing $(-\varepsilon, 2\varepsilon)$ instead would give $\log2 -
\log2 = 0$, so the value of the "integral" depends on the prescription, which is why the principal value must be
named.
:::

The Sokhotski-Plemelj formula is the rule for evaluating integrals with a pole displaced slightly off the real
axis, and it is used in every propagator with an $i\epsilon$. The second example checks the two halves of the
formula and gives a first application.

::: {#exm-dist-pv-plemelj}
#### The $i\varepsilon$ prescription

$\int\frac{\varepsilon}{x^2 + \varepsilon^2}dx = \pi$ for every $\varepsilon > 0$ (@prp-distribution-identities),
and the Lorentzian concentrates at $0$, so $\frac{\varepsilon}{x^2 + \varepsilon^2} \to \pi\delta$; and
$\int\frac{x\varphi(x)}{x^2 + \varepsilon^2}dx = \int_0^\infty\frac{x(\varphi(x) - \varphi(-x))}{x^2 +
\varepsilon^2}dx \to \operatorname{PV}\frac1x(\varphi)$ by dominated convergence. Hence
$\lim\int\frac{\varphi(x)}{x - i\varepsilon}dx = \operatorname{PV}\int\frac{\varphi}{x} + i\pi\varphi(0)$; for
$\varphi$ real this says that the imaginary part of the $i\varepsilon$-regularised integral is $\pi$ times the
value at the pole, the rule behind the optical theorem and the imaginary parts of propagators.
:::

The Fourier transform of the principal value is a step: the sine integral gives $\pi$ times the sign of the
frequency, and the cosine integral vanishes by oddness. The third example records this transform and the one of
the sign function that follows from it.

::: {#exm-dist-pv-transform}
#### The transform of $\operatorname{PV}1/x$

$\operatorname{PV}\int\frac{e^{-ikx}}{x}dx = -i\operatorname{PV}\int\frac{\sin kx}{x}dx = -i\pi\operatorname{sgn}k$
(@prp-distribution-identities), since the cosine part is odd and the Dirichlet integral $\int\frac{\sin kx}{x}dx =
\pi\operatorname{sgn}k$ needs no principal value. By duality (@thm-fourier-inversion, extended to distributions in
@def-distribution-transform), $\widehat{\operatorname{sgn}x} = \frac{2}{ik} = -\frac{2i}{k}$ as a principal
value, and $\hat\theta = \pi\delta(k) + \frac{1}{ik}$ from $\theta = \tfrac12(1 + \operatorname{sgn})$, the
transform of the step that appears in every retarded Green's function.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
Principal-value integrals through a pole can be computed by Sage as symmetric limits, and comparing with the
residue theorem shows the half-residue rule. The first exercise does three such integrals and interprets the
third by @thm-residue.

::: {#exr-dist-pv}
#### Principal values in Sage

Compute $\operatorname{PV}\int_{-1}^3\frac{dx}{x}$, $\operatorname{PV}\int_{-\infty}^\infty\frac{dx}{x(x^2 + 1)}$
and $\operatorname{PV}\int_{-\infty}^\infty\frac{\cos x}{x - 1}dx$ as symmetric limits with Sage, and explain the
third by the residue theorem with the pole on the contour.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\log3$; $0$ by oddness; and $-\pi\sin1$: with $x = y + 1$ the integrand is $\frac{\cos y\cos1 - \sin y\sin1}{y}$,
the principal value of the odd function $\cos y/y$ vanishes, and $\int\frac{\sin y}{y}dy = \pi$ (Maxima refuses
the conditionally convergent integral in its original form, so Sage is given the shifted one). By the residue
theorem, the integral is $\operatorname{Re}\operatorname{PV}\int\frac{e^{ix}}{x - 1}dx$, and a small semicircle
around the pole on the contour contributes half the residue $e^{i}$, giving $i\pi e^{i} = i\pi\cos1 - \pi\sin1$
(closing in the upper half-plane, where no other pole lies), whose real part is $-\pi\sin1$:

{{< sage exr-dist-pv >}}
:::

The identification of the principal value as the derivative of the logarithm is what makes it unavoidable: a
locally integrable function has a derivative, and this is it. The second exercise proves the identification and
the product identity.

::: {#exr-dist-pv-log}
#### The derivative of $\log|x|$

Show that $\log|x|$ is a tempered distribution and that its derivative is $\operatorname{PV}\frac1x$; show that
$x\cdot\operatorname{PV}\frac1x = 1$ and that the general solution of $xT = 1$ is $\operatorname{PV}\frac1x +
c\,\delta$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\log|x|$ is locally integrable ($\int_0^1|\log x|dx = 1$) and of logarithmic growth, hence tempered. By
definition, $(\log|x|)'(\varphi) = -\int\log|x|\varphi'(x)dx = -\lim_{\varepsilon \to 0}\int_{|x| >
\varepsilon}\log|x|\varphi'$, and integrating by parts on each half-line, $-\int_{|x| > \varepsilon}\log|x|\varphi'
= \int_{|x| > \varepsilon}\frac{\varphi}{x}dx + \log\varepsilon\,[\varphi(\varepsilon) - \varphi(-\varepsilon)]$; the
boundary term is $O(\varepsilon\log\varepsilon) \to 0$ and the integral tends to the principal value. $(x\cdot
\operatorname{PV}\frac1x)(\varphi) = \lim\int_{|x| > \varepsilon}\frac{x\varphi(x)}{x}dx = \int\varphi$, so the
product is $1$. If $xT = 1$ then $x(T - \operatorname{PV}\frac1x) = 0$, and a distribution $S$ with $xS = 0$
satisfies $S(\varphi) = 0$ for every $\varphi$ vanishing at $0$ (write $\varphi = x\psi$ with $\psi$ smooth), so
$S(\varphi)$ depends only on $\varphi(0)$ and $S = c\delta$ by @exr-dist-not-function.
:::

The principal value of $1/x^2$ does not exist as a symmetric limit, and the right object is the derivative of
the principal value of $1/x$, a finite part. The third exercise defines it and computes its action, which
subtracts the value of the test function at the origin.

::: {#exr-dist-finite-part}
#### The finite part of $1/x^2$

Define $\operatorname{Pf}\frac{1}{x^2} = -\bigl(\operatorname{PV}\frac1x\bigr)'$. Show that
$\operatorname{Pf}\frac{1}{x^2}(\varphi) = \lim_{\varepsilon \to 0}\Bigl[\int_{|x| > \varepsilon}\frac{\varphi(x)}{x^2}dx -
\frac{2\varphi(0)}{\varepsilon}\Bigr] = \int_0^\infty\frac{\varphi(x) + \varphi(-x) - 2\varphi(0)}{x^2}dx$, that
$x^2\operatorname{Pf}\frac{1}{x^2} = 1$, and compute $\operatorname{Pf}\frac{1}{x^2}(e^{-x^2})$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$-(\operatorname{PV}\frac1x)'(\varphi) = \operatorname{PV}\frac1x(\varphi') = \lim\int_{|x| >
\varepsilon}\frac{\varphi'}{x}$, and integrating by parts on each half-line gives $\lim\bigl[\int_{|x| >
\varepsilon}\frac{\varphi}{x^2} + \frac{\varphi(\varepsilon) + \varphi(-\varepsilon)}{\varepsilon}\cdot(-1)\bigr]$,
where $\varphi(\pm\varepsilon) = \varphi(0) \pm \varepsilon\varphi'(0) + O(\varepsilon^2)$ gives
$-2\varphi(0)/\varepsilon + O(\varepsilon)$; the symmetric form follows by pairing $x$ with $-x$, the integrand
being bounded near $0$ by $\sup|\varphi''|$. Multiplying by $x^2$ removes the singularity and the subtraction, so
$x^2\operatorname{Pf}\frac{1}{x^2} = 1$. For $\varphi = e^{-x^2}$, $2\int_0^\infty\frac{e^{-x^2} - 1}{x^2}dx =
2\Bigl[\frac{1 - e^{-x^2}}{x}\Bigr]_0^\infty - 2\int_0^\infty\frac{2xe^{-x^2}}{x}dx = -4\cdot\frac{\sqrt\pi}{2} =
-2\sqrt\pi$, after integrating by parts (@sec-riemann-integral).
:::

### The Fourier transform of distributions

Since the transform is a continuous bijection of the Schwartz space, it can be moved onto the test function, and
every tempered distribution acquires a transform. The definition does this and lists the transforms of the delta,
the constant, the plane wave and their derivatives, the dictionary used in every momentum-space computation.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-distribution-transform}
#### Fourier transform of a distribution

The **Fourier transform** of a tempered distribution $T$ is the tempered distribution $\hat T(\varphi) = T(\hat
\varphi)$, which agrees with @eq-fourier-transform for integrable $f$ by Fubini, since $\int f(x)\hat\varphi(x)dx =
\int\hat f(k)\varphi(k)dk$. The rules of @def-fourier-transform persist, $\widehat{T'} = ik\hat T$, $\widehat{xT}
= i\hat T\,'$, $\widehat{T(x - a)} = e^{-ika}\hat T$, as does inversion $\hat{\hat T} = 2\pi T(-x)$. The basic
transforms are
$$
\hat\delta = 1, \qquad \hat 1 = 2\pi\delta(k), \qquad \widehat{e^{iax}} = 2\pi\delta(k - a), \qquad
\widehat{\delta^{(n)}} = (ik)^n, \qquad \widehat{x^n} = 2\pi i^n\delta^{(n)}(k),
$$ {#eq-delta-transforms}
and the second of these is the identity $\int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-ikx}dx = 2\pi\delta(k)$ that physicists use to
enforce momentum conservation; the Fourier series of a periodic function $f = \sum c_ne^{inx}$ is its transform
$\hat f = 2\pi\sum_nc_n\delta(k - n)$, a sum of deltas at the integers.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The transform of the delta is the constant $1$, the statement that a point source contains all wave numbers
equally. The first example computes it from the definition and reads off the transforms of the derivatives of
the delta.

::: {#exm-dist-ft-delta}
#### $\hat\delta = 1$

$\hat\delta(\varphi) = \delta(\hat\varphi) = \hat\varphi(0) = \int\varphi(x)dx = 1(\varphi)$, so $\hat\delta = 1$;
and $\widehat{\delta_a}(\varphi) = \hat\varphi(a) = \int\varphi e^{-iax}$, so $\widehat{\delta(x - a)} =
e^{-ika}$, a pure phase. By the derivative rule $\widehat{\delta'} = ik$, consistent with
$\widehat{\delta'}(\varphi) = -\hat\varphi\,'(0) = \int ix\varphi(x)dx$ after renaming $x$ to $k$. The white
spectrum of the delta is the limit of the Gaussian transforms $e^{-\varepsilon^2k^2/4}$ of $g_\varepsilon$, which
tend to $1$ as $\varepsilon \to 0$.
:::

The transform of the constant is a delta, by inversion from the previous example or as a limit of ever wider
Gaussian transforms. The second example gives both arguments, and the version with the kernel $\sin(Lx)/\pi x$
of @fig-delta-sequence.

::: {#exm-dist-ft-constant}
#### $\hat 1 = 2\pi\delta$

From $\hat\delta = 1$ and inversion, $\hat 1 = \hat{\hat\delta} = 2\pi\delta(-k) = 2\pi\delta(k)$. As a limit,
the transform of $e^{-\varepsilon x^2}$ is $\sqrt{\pi/\varepsilon}\,e^{-k^2/4\varepsilon}$, a Gaussian of unit
integral times $2\pi$, which tends to $2\pi\delta$ (@exr-dist-ft-constant); and truncating instead of damping,
$\int_{-L}^Le^{-ikx}dx = \frac{2\sin Lk}{k} = 2\pi\delta_L(k) \to 2\pi\delta(k)$ by @fig-delta-sequence
(@prp-distribution-identities). Modulating, $\widehat{e^{iax}} = 2\pi\delta(k - a)$: a plane wave has a single
wave number.
:::

A periodic function is a tempered distribution whose transform is a comb of deltas weighted by its Fourier
coefficients, which unifies the two kinds of Fourier analysis. The third example works this out and transforms
the Dirac comb itself.

::: {#exm-dist-ft-periodic}
#### Periodic functions and the comb

If $f = \sum_nc_ne^{inx}$ converges as distributions (which it does for every piecewise continuous periodic $f$),
then $\hat f = \sum_nc_n\widehat{e^{inx}} = 2\pi\sum_nc_n\delta(k - n)$: the spectrum of a periodic function is
supported on the integers with weights $2\pi c_n$. For the Dirac comb $\text{Ш} = \frac{1}{2\pi}\sum e^{inx}$ of
@exr-dist-comb, all $c_n = 1/2\pi$ and $\hat{\text{Ш}} = \sum_n\delta(k - n)$: the comb of spacing $2\pi$
transforms to the comb of spacing $1$, and pairing with $\varphi$ gives Poisson summation once more.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The limit $\hat 1 = 2\pi\delta$ can be watched in Sage by transforming damped constants and integrating the
results against test functions. The first exercise does this for Gaussian and exponential damping, exactly in the
damping parameter.

::: {#exr-dist-ft-constant}
#### $\hat 1$ as a limit

Compute the transforms of $e^{-\varepsilon x^2}$ and of $e^{-\varepsilon|x|}$ with Sage, integrate the first
against $\varphi(k) = e^{-k^2/2}$ and $\varphi(k) = \cos k$ and the second against $\varphi(k) = \cos k$ and
$\varphi(k) = 1/(1 + k^2)$, and take $\varepsilon \to 0$ to confirm $2\pi\varphi(0)$ in all four cases.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The transforms are $\sqrt{\pi/\varepsilon}e^{-k^2/4\varepsilon}$ and $2\varepsilon/(\varepsilon^2 + k^2)$, both of
integral $2\pi$ and both concentrating at $k = 0$; the four integrals are $2\pi/\sqrt{1 + 2\varepsilon}$,
$2\pi e^{-\varepsilon}$, $2\pi e^{-\varepsilon}$ and $2\pi/(1 + \varepsilon)$, all tending to $2\pi =
2\pi\varphi(0)$:

{{< sage exr-dist-ft-constant >}}
:::

The transform rules extend to distributions by moving everything onto the test function, and the second exercise
asks for the derivations of the two most used ones. It then applies them to obtain the transforms of $x^n$ and of
the derivatives of the delta.

::: {#exr-dist-ft-rules}
#### Rules for distributions

Prove $\widehat{T'} = ik\hat T$ and $\widehat{xT} = i\hat T\,'$ for tempered distributions from the corresponding
rules on Schwartz functions, and deduce $\widehat{\delta^{(n)}} = (ik)^n$ and $\widehat{x^n} = 2\pi
i^n\delta^{(n)}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\widehat{T'}(\varphi) = T'(\hat\varphi) = -T(\hat\varphi\,')$, and the multiplication rule for $\varphi$ gives
$\hat\varphi\,' = -i\,\widehat{x\varphi}$, so $-T(\hat\varphi\,') = T(\widehat{ix\varphi}) = \hat T(ix\varphi) =
(ik\hat T)(\varphi)$ after renaming the variable. Similarly $\widehat{xT}(\varphi) = T(x\hat\varphi)$, and the derivative
rule $\widehat{\varphi'} = ik\hat\varphi$ gives $k\hat\varphi = \widehat{-i\varphi'}$, so $T(x\hat\varphi) =
\hat T(-i\varphi') = -i\hat T(\varphi') = i\hat T\,'(\varphi)$. Iterating the first on $\hat\delta = 1$ gives
$(ik)^n$; iterating the second on $\hat1 = 2\pi\delta$ gives $\widehat{x^n} = i^n\cdot2\pi\delta^{(n)}$.
:::

The sign function and the step function have transforms that mix a principal value with a delta, and they can be
obtained as limits of damped versions. The third exercise derives them this way, with Sage producing the damped
transforms, and uses the Sokhotski-Plemelj formula to combine the two pieces.

::: {#exr-dist-ft-sign}
#### The transforms of $\operatorname{sgn}$ and $\theta$

Compute the transform of $\operatorname{sgn}(x)e^{-\varepsilon|x|}$ with Sage and let $\varepsilon \to 0$ to show
$\widehat{\operatorname{sgn}} = -2i\operatorname{PV}\frac1k$; deduce $\hat\theta = \pi\delta(k) +
\frac{1}{i}\operatorname{PV}\frac1k$, and show that this equals $\lim_{\varepsilon \to 0}\frac{1}{i(k -
i\varepsilon)}$, the transform of $\theta(x)e^{-\varepsilon x}$ of @exr-ft-one-sided.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The damped transform is $\frac{1}{\varepsilon + ik} - \frac{1}{\varepsilon - ik} = \frac{-2ik}{\varepsilon^2 +
k^2}$, which tends to $-2i\operatorname{PV}\frac1k$ by @exm-dist-pv-plemelj. Then $\theta = \tfrac12(1 +
\operatorname{sgn})$ gives $\hat\theta = \pi\delta(k) - i\operatorname{PV}\frac1k = \pi\delta(k) +
\frac1i\operatorname{PV}\frac1k$. On the other hand $\widehat{\theta e^{-\varepsilon x}} = \frac{1}{\varepsilon + ik}
= \frac{1}{i(k - i\varepsilon)}$, and the Sokhotski-Plemelj formula @eq-sokhotski-plemelj gives
$\frac{1}{i}\bigl(\operatorname{PV}\frac1k + i\pi\delta\bigr) = \frac1i\operatorname{PV}\frac1k + \pi\delta$, the
same distribution: the two regularisations agree, as they must:

{{< sage exr-dist-ft-sign >}}
:::

### Worked computations

The distributional identities of this section are statements about limits of ordinary integrals, each obtained
by computing the integral exactly as a function of the parameter and then taking the limit. The proposition lists
them.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-distribution-identities}
#### Delta sequences, derivatives and principal values

The Gaussians $g_\varepsilon$ have unit integral; $\int g_\varepsilon\cos x = e^{-\varepsilon^2/4} \to 1$ and $\int
g_\varepsilon(x^2 + 1) = 1 + \varepsilon^2/2 \to 1$; $\int g_\varepsilon'\sin x = -e^{-\varepsilon^2/4} \to -1$ and
$\int xg_\varepsilon'\cos x \to -1$ (the identities $\delta'(\varphi) = -\varphi'(0)$ and $x\delta' = -\delta$);
$-\int_0^\infty f' = f(0)$ for $f = (1 + x)e^{-x^2}$ ($\theta' = \delta$); $\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-L}^Le^{ikx}dk =
\sin(Lx)/\pi x$ has unit integral and $\int\frac{\sin Lx}{\pi x}\cos x\,dx = 1$ exactly for $L > 1$;
$\operatorname{PV}\int_{-1}^2dx/x = \log2$; $\int\frac{\varepsilon}{x^2 + \varepsilon^2}dx = \pi$ and $\int\frac{\sin
kx}{x}dx = \pi\operatorname{sgn}k$.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
A limit of distributions is computed by keeping the parameter free, integrating exactly and taking the limit
afterwards, never by substituting a small number. The first example explains this order of operations and why it
is the faithful translation of the definition.

::: {#exm-dist-sage-limit}
#### Limits of parametric integrals

For every $\varepsilon > 0$, $\int g_\varepsilon(x)\cos x\,dx = e^{-\varepsilon^2/4}$, the real part of the
Gaussian transform at $k = 1$; its limit as $\varepsilon \to 0$ is $1 = \cos 0$. This is exactly
$\lim_\varepsilon T_{g_\varepsilon}(\varphi)$, the definition of convergence of distributions applied to the test
function $\cos x$. Substituting $\varepsilon = 10^{-3}$ first would give $0.99999975\ldots$, a number close to $1$
but no proof of the limit.
:::

The principal value is a limit of two ordinary integrals that leave out a small symmetric interval around the
pole. The second example computes $\operatorname{PV}\int_{-1}^2dx/x$, where the divergent parts cancel before the
limit is taken, and the integral of the Lorentzian.

::: {#exm-dist-sage-pv}
#### Computing a principal value

For $0 < \varepsilon < 1$, so that the excised interval lies inside $[-1, 2]$, $\int_{-1}^{-\varepsilon}\frac{dx}{x} +
\int_\varepsilon^2\frac{dx}{x} = \log\varepsilon + (\log2 - \log\varepsilon) = \log2$: the sum is $\log2$
before the limit is even taken, which is the cancellation of @exm-dist-pv-rational. For the Lorentzian,
$\int\frac{\varepsilon}{x^2 + \varepsilon^2}dx = \bigl[\arctan(x/\varepsilon)\bigr]_{-\infty}^\infty = \pi$ for every
$\varepsilon > 0$.
:::

The Dirichlet integral with a parameter is a sign function, and it expresses the transform of the principal
value. The third example records this and the one case where the value at the origin needs care.

::: {#exm-dist-sage-sgn}
#### The sign function in the output

For real $k \neq 0$ the substitution $t = |k|x$ gives $\int\frac{\sin kx}{x}dx = \operatorname{sgn}(k)\int\frac{\sin
t}{t}dt = \pi\operatorname{sgn}k$, the transform $i\,\widehat{\operatorname{PV}1/x}$ of @exm-dist-pv-transform; at
$k = 0$ the integrand vanishes and $\operatorname{sgn}0 = 0$ gives the right value. For the Fourier kernel,
$\frac{\sin Lx\cos x}{\pi x} = \frac{\sin(L + 1)x + \sin(L - 1)x}{2\pi x}$ integrates to
$\tfrac12[\operatorname{sgn}(L + 1) + \operatorname{sgn}(L - 1)]$, which is $1$ for $L > 1$.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
Sequences converging to $\delta'$ need not be derivatives of delta sequences, and the difference of two shifted
Gaussians is the physicist's dipole. The first exercise shows that it converges to $\delta'$ and compares the
rate with that of $g_\varepsilon'$.

::: {#exr-dist-delta-prime}
#### Dipole sequences

Show that $d_\varepsilon(x) = [g_\varepsilon(x + \varepsilon) - g_\varepsilon(x - \varepsilon)]/2\varepsilon$ and
$g_\varepsilon'(x)$ both converge to $\delta'$ by computing $\int d_\varepsilon\varphi$ and $\int
g_\varepsilon'\varphi$ exactly for $\varphi = x$, $x^3$ and $\sin x$ with Sage, and compare the orders in
$\varepsilon$ of the two errors.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Both tend to $-\varphi'(0) = -1, 0, -1$; the errors of $g_\varepsilon'$ are $O(\varepsilon^2)$ while those of the
dipole are $O(\varepsilon^2)$ too but with larger constants, since the finite difference adds an error
$\varepsilon^2\varphi'''(0)/6$ of its own, visible for $\varphi = x^3$, where $\int g_\varepsilon'x^3 = -
\tfrac32\varepsilon^2$ but $\int d_\varepsilon x^3 = -\tfrac32\varepsilon^2 - \varepsilon^2$:

{{< sage exr-dist-delta-prime >}}
:::

The heat kernel is the delta sequence that solves the heat equation, and the solution with a point source is the
kernel itself. The second exercise verifies the delta limit against test functions and interprets the result for
the heat equation of @def-heat-equation.

::: {#exr-dist-heat-kernel-delta}
#### The heat kernel as a delta sequence

Show with Sage that $K_t(x) = e^{-x^2/4\kappa t}/\sqrt{4\pi\kappa t}$ has unit integral, that $\int K_t\varphi \to
\varphi(0)$ as $t \to 0^+$ for $\varphi = \cos x$ and $\varphi = x^2 + x + 1$, and that $\int K_tx^2\,dx = 2\kappa
t$; interpret the last result.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\int K_t\cos x = e^{-\kappa t} \to 1$ and $\int K_t(x^2 + x + 1) = 1 + 2\kappa t \to 1$; the second moment
$2\kappa t$ is the mean square distance travelled by heat (or by a diffusing particle) in time $t$, growing
linearly in $t$, which is the signature of diffusion as opposed to the $t^2$ of ballistic motion. The solution of
$u_t = \kappa u_{xx}$ with $u(0, x) = \delta(x)$ is $K_t$ itself, by @exm-ft-convolution-heat with $u_0 = \delta$
and $\hat\delta = 1$:

{{< sage exr-dist-heat-kernel-delta >}}
:::
